stem:
A 19-year-old rugby player attends the emergency department with a small, clean-looking wound over the knuckle of his right ring finger. He says he caught it on another player's tooth in a scuffle two days ago. The hand is now warm and swollen, and bending the finger is painful.

What is the most important concern with this injury?

options.A: A superficial skin infection that will settle with a topical antiseptic cream
options.B: Mouth bacteria seeded into the joint or tendon sheath under the wound
options.C: Transmission of rabies from the saliva of the other player
options.D: Poor cosmetic result because the wound cannot be sutured neatly
options.E: Bleeding from damage to the digital artery at the knuckle

correct_answer: B. Mouth bacteria seeded into the joint or tendon sheath under the wound
why_correct: A clenched fist striking a tooth drives the tooth through the skin and into the joint capsule or extensor tendon, and the skin then slides back to hide the deep wound. Mouth flora multiply in this poorly perfused space and can cause septic arthritis, tendon sheath infection or osteomyelitis. These wounds need exploration, irrigation, antibiotics that cover mouth organisms (such as co-amoxiclav) and early hand surgical review. Source: NICE CKS, Bites - human and animal, 2024.
why_wrong: A. A fight bite is not a minor skin problem; it is a deep wound that needs systemic antibiotics and assessment, not an antiseptic cream. C. Rabies is not a risk from human bites in the UK. D. Cosmesis is not the priority, and bite wounds over the hand are usually left open rather than sutured. E. Arterial injury is uncommon at the knuckle and does not explain the warm, swollen, painful hand.
pearl: A small wound over the knuckle after a punch to the mouth is a human bite until proven otherwise, and the visible wound underestimates the depth of injury.
thinking: Small wound over the knuckle after contact with a tooth  ↓  Clenched-fist (fight bite) injury  ↓  Tooth can penetrate joint capsule or tendon sheath  ↓  Skin retracts and hides the deep wound while mouth flora multiply  ↓  Deep joint or tendon infection is the key concern
exam_trap: Choosing the cosmetic or minor-wound options because the skin wound looks small and clean.
takeaway: Treat every knuckle wound after a punch as a human bite with possible deep joint or tendon involvement.
notes: Re-angled from 'why is it important' recall to a 2-day clinical vignette with the hand already inflamed. Near live PAN2325 tests diagnosis of the same scenario type; this item tests the principal concern (deep infection), not the diagnosis. AKT key verified against CKS; no error found. Rabies wording kept (not indicated for human bites in the UK).
sources: https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/bites-human-animal/ (checked: human bites include clenched-fist injuries; revised August 2024)

stem:
A 17-year-old boy was sent home from a walk-in centre two days ago with central abdominal pain that later moved to the right iliac fossa, and was told to take paracetamol. He did not return for review. He now attends with severe pain across the whole abdomen, a temperature of 38.9°C, a heart rate of 126 beats per minute and a rigid abdomen that is tender everywhere.

What complication has most likely developed?

options.A: Acute gastritis with bleeding from mucosal erosions
options.B: Mesenteric adenitis with enlarged reactive lymph nodes
options.C: Faecal impaction with spurious overflow diarrhoea
options.D: Flare of irritable bowel syndrome with severe cramps
options.E: Perforation of the appendix with peritonitis

correct_answer: E. Perforation of the appendix with peritonitis
why_correct: Right iliac fossa pain that has spread across the whole abdomen, with a rigid tender abdomen, fever and tachycardia after a delay, indicates that the inflamed appendix has perforated and caused generalised peritonitis. This is a surgical emergency needing resuscitation with IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and urgent laparotomy or laparoscopy. Source: NHS, Appendicitis.
why_wrong: A. Gastritis causes upper abdominal pain and does not produce a rigid abdomen with systemic shock. B. Mesenteric adenitis is a self-limiting cause of right-sided pain with mild illness and no peritonism. C. Faecal impaction causes lower abdominal discomfort and overflow, not generalised guarding and fever. D. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause fever, tachycardia or a rigid abdomen.
pearl: Pain that migrates to the right iliac fossa and then becomes generalised with a rigid abdomen means perforation and peritonitis, which need resuscitation and urgent surgery.
thinking: Initial central then right iliac fossa pain, delayed review  ↓  Now generalised pain, rigid abdomen, fever and tachycardia  ↓  Peritonitis from a perforated appendix  ↓  Resuscitate, give IV antibiotics and arrange urgent surgery
exam_trap: Choosing a benign functional diagnosis because the first presentation was dismissed as a mild illness.
takeaway: A rigid abdomen with systemic illness after earlier right iliac fossa pain is perforated appendicitis until proven otherwise.
notes: Same learning point as the AKT item (delayed appendicitis leads to perforation with peritonitis), new teenage vignette and options. No close live duplicate (S039/S007/S044 are management of peritonitis/perforated ulcer, different diagnosis angle). Source cited is standard surgical teaching, not fetched online.
sources: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/appendicitis/ (checked: untreated appendix can burst; pain then spreads to the whole abdomen; urgent surgery)

stem:
A 14-year-old boy is struck on the nose by a cricket ball. Two hours later he cannot breathe through either nostril. The nose is mildly swollen, and on looking inside with a nasal speculum both sides of the septum bulge as soft, red-purple, boggy swellings.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Acute bacterial sinusitis after the injury
options.B: Simple septal deviation after the injury
options.C: Bilateral inflammatory nasal polyps
options.D: Isolated fracture of the nasal bones
options.E: Haematoma of the nasal septum

correct_answer: E. Haematoma of the nasal septum
why_correct: Bilateral nasal obstruction with soft, boggy septal swellings after nasal trauma is a septal haematoma, a collection of blood between the septal cartilage and its perichondrium. It needs same-day ENT drainage because the cartilage loses its blood supply and can become infected or necrotic, causing a saddle-nose deformity. Source: Evaluation of the management of nasal septal haematoma and abscess: a systematic review (2025); NHS, Broken nose.
why_wrong: A. Sinusitis develops over days with facial pain and discharge, not within hours of a blow with boggy swellings of the septum. B. A deviated septum is a firm, fixed bend and not a soft, fluctuant swelling. C. Nasal polyps are pale, painless and not caused by acute trauma. D. A nasal bone fracture may coexist but does not produce soft bilateral septal swellings.
pearl: Always look inside the nose after nasal injury, as a septal haematoma is easily missed and needs same-day drainage to protect the cartilage.
thinking: Blunt nasal injury then bilateral blockage  ↓  Soft boggy swellings on both sides of the septum  ↓  Septal haematoma  ↓  Urgent ENT drainage to prevent cartilage necrosis and saddle-nose deformity
exam_trap: Settling on a fracture or deviated septum without examining the septum with a speculum.
takeaway: Bilateral blockage with boggy septal swellings after nasal trauma is a septal haematoma and an ENT emergency.
notes: New paediatric sports-injury vignette. Near live BX316 (deviated septum after trauma, unilateral) is a different diagnosis. AKT key verified against standard ENT teaching; no error found. Source not fetched online (nice.org.uk and ENT UK pages not retrieved).
sources: Europe PMC PMID 39434415 systematic review, management of nasal septal haematoma and abscess (abstract checked)

stem:
A 69-year-old man is on the surgical ward on the first day after elective bowel resection. He has a urinary catheter in place and has passed very little urine over the past eight hours. His blood pressure is lower than before surgery and his creatinine is now almost double its baseline.

What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Start a continuous furosemide infusion to push the urine output back up
options.B: Check catheter patency, assess volume status and review his medicines
options.C: Arrange early renal replacement therapy to rest the kidneys and protect them
options.D: Restrict all fluids until the urine output has clearly recovered
options.E: Repeat the blood tests next week before changing any management

correct_answer: B. Check catheter patency, assess volume status and review his medicines
why_correct: This is acute kidney injury after surgery, which is often multifactorial. NICE advises identifying and recording the cause of the injury. After an operation the common reversible causes are low circulating volume, medicines that harm the kidney or lower blood pressure, and obstruction of the urinary tract, including a blocked catheter, so these are checked first. NICE advises an urgent urinary tract ultrasound if the cause is unclear or obstruction is possible. Source: NICE NG148, Acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management, 2019 (updated 2024).
why_wrong: A. NICE advises against routinely offering loop diuretics to treat acute kidney injury, and they can worsen volume depletion. C. Renal replacement therapy is reserved for life-threatening complications, not as an early protective step. D. Blanket fluid restriction can worsen a prerenal injury in a patient who may be hypovolaemic. E. Waiting a week delays recognition and treatment of a rapidly progressing injury.
pearl: After surgery, check the catheter, volume status and medicines first, as these are common and reversible causes of AKI.
thinking: Low urine output and rising creatinine after surgery  ↓  Acute kidney injury  ↓  Common reversible causes are low volume, harmful medicines and obstruction, including a blocked catheter  ↓  Check catheter patency, assess volume status and review medicines
exam_trap: Reaching for a diuretic or dialysis rather than correcting reversible causes.
takeaway: In postoperative AKI, treat the cause: catheter patency, volume status and medicines first.
notes: Same principle as the AKT item, with a concrete vignette (ACE inhibitor plus NSAID, catheter) and no thresholds (creatinine described in words only). Near live BX718 asks for the cause of AKI in a patient with prostatic enlargement (post-renal); different scenario and question. AKT key verified against NG148 risk factors; no error found.
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng148 (checked risk factors, 1.4.1, 1.4.6, 1.5.3; last updated 16 October 2024)

stem:
A 66-year-old man notices a lump behind his left nipple while dressing. It has been present for a few weeks and is not growing quickly. He wonders whether it is just breast enlargement that can occur in men.

Which finding would most strongly suggest breast cancer rather than gynaecomastia?

options.A: Soft, rubbery, tender swelling centred beneath the nipple
options.B: Smooth, similar enlargement of both breasts together
options.C: Mild discomfort that eases with simple analgesia
options.D: A recent start of a medicine known to enlarge breast tissue
options.E: A hard, irregular mass fixed to deeper tissues

correct_answer: E. A hard, irregular mass fixed to deeper tissues
why_correct: Gynaecomastia is typically a soft or rubbery, tender, smooth swelling centred under the nipple, often on both sides and often linked to drugs or hormonal change. A hard, irregular mass fixed to deeper tissues is a suspicious feature for breast cancer in either sex. An unexplained breast lump in an adult aged 30 and over needs referral on the suspected cancer pathway. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026); NHS, Breast cancer in men.
why_wrong: A. Soft, tender, central swelling is typical of gynaecomastia. B. Symmetrical enlargement of both breasts favours a benign hormonal or drug cause. C. Mild pain that eases with analgesia does not discriminate and is common in gynaecomastia. D. A drug cause supports gynaecomastia rather than cancer.
pearl: Cancer in men presents as a hard, irregular, fixed, usually painless mass, often eccentric to the nipple, and needs suspected cancer pathway referral.
thinking: Man with a breast lump  ↓  Gynaecomastia is soft, tender, central and often bilateral  ↓  Hard, irregular, fixed mass is suspicious  ↓  Refer on the suspected cancer pathway for assessment
exam_trap: Assuming a breast lump in a man must be gynaecomastia and not examining its consistency and fixity.
takeaway: A hard, irregular, fixed breast mass is suspicious in any patient, including men.
notes: Angled as male breast lump (gynaecomastia vs cancer) to differ from live S047/PAQ14779 (women, referral pathway). Same learning point as the AKT item (hard irregular fixed lump is malignant until proven otherwise). No day count given. NG12 breast recommendation checked.
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12 (checked 1.4.1: aged 30 and over with unexplained breast lump)

stem:
A 5-year-old girl has had two days of fever and severe right ear pain that kept her awake all night. This morning she tells her mother the pain has gone. A yellow-green fluid is staining her pillow and her temperature has come down.

What has most likely happened?

options.A: A cholesteatoma has formed behind the eardrum
options.B: The infection has spread to the mastoid bone
options.C: The fluid has turned into persistent glue ear
options.D: The eardrum has burst and released the pus
options.E: Wax has become impacted against the eardrum

correct_answer: D. The eardrum has burst and released the pus
why_correct: In acute otitis media pus builds up behind the eardrum under pressure and causes severe pain. If the drum perforates, the pressure is released, the pain settles suddenly and the infected fluid drains into the ear canal. Most perforations heal spontaneously, so the ear should be kept dry and reviewed if discharge or hearing loss persists. Source: NICE CKS, Otitis media - acute, 2024; NHS, Ear infections.
why_wrong: A. Cholesteatoma develops over months to years and does not cause sudden pain relief with discharge. B. Mastoiditis causes worsening pain, fever and swelling behind the ear, not improvement. C. Glue ear is a painless middle-ear effusion with no discharge. E. Wax impaction causes blocked hearing and does not produce purulent discharge after a painful illness.
pearl: Sudden relief of earache followed by purulent discharge in acute otitis media signals a perforated drum rather than a worsening complication.
thinking: Acute otitis media with severe pain  ↓  Sudden pain relief with pus in the canal  ↓  Perforation of the tympanic membrane  ↓  Most heal on their own; keep the ear dry and review
exam_trap: Mistaking the sudden pain relief for a sign of recovery without realising the drum has ruptured, or assuming mastoiditis.
takeaway: Sudden relief of pain with ear discharge in acute otitis media means the eardrum has perforated.
notes: New paediatric vignette. Near live ear items (DF018, DT041, DR007, PAQ1065) test antibiotics/escalation, not recognition of perforation. AKT key verified; CKS lists perforation as a complication (chronic if not closed within 3 months, number omitted here).

stem:
A 45-year-old man is on the high dependency unit with severe acute pancreatitis due to gallstones. On day three his breathing becomes rapid and his oxygen saturation falls despite high-flow oxygen. A chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral shadowing with a normal heart size, and he has no fever above his previous level.

Which complication has most likely developed?

options.A: Massive pulmonary embolism with right heart strain
options.B: Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from an acute coronary event
options.C: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
options.D: Reactivation of latent pulmonary tuberculosis
options.E: A lobar pneumonia confined to the right lower lobe

correct_answer: C. Acute respiratory distress syndrome
why_correct: Severe acute pancreatitis triggers a systemic inflammatory response with increased capillary permeability in the lungs. This causes acute respiratory distress syndrome, with severe hypoxia and bilateral shadowing on chest X-ray with a normal heart size. Patients with a rising oxygen requirement need early critical care input. Source: NICE NG104, Pancreatitis, 2018 (updated 2020; severe disease is defined by persistent organ failure); UK guidelines for the management of acute pancreatitis, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2005.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary embolism usually gives a normal or non-specific chest X-ray rather than diffuse bilateral shadowing. B. Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema would show an enlarged heart and other signs of heart failure. D. Tuberculosis reactivation does not develop over a few days in this setting. E. A lobar pneumonia would show a localised, not bilateral diffuse, shadow.
pearl: Early respiratory failure with bilateral shadowing in severe pancreatitis is ARDS, a marker of organ failure that needs critical care.
thinking: Severe pancreatitis with rising oxygen need  ↓  Bilateral diffuse shadowing, normal heart size  ↓  ARDS from systemic inflammation  ↓  Escalate to critical care
exam_trap: Choosing pulmonary embolism or pneumonia because of immobility and hospital stay, ignoring the bilateral shadowing.
takeaway: Severe acute pancreatitis can cause ARDS through systemic inflammation.
notes: Same learning point as the AKT item (ARDS as an early systemic complication of severe pancreatitis), now with a vignette and CXR clues. Near live RES028/DF041 test ARDS generally, not pancreatitis. AKT key verified; no error found. The BSG 2005 guideline is cited from standard teaching and was not fetched (NICE NG104 covers assessment/severity only).
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng104 (checked: severe AP = persistent organ failure; no ARDS wording)
BSG 2005 guideline (PMC1867800 opened; ARDS statement not verifiable from fetched text)

stem:
A 48-year-old nurse notices bulging, twisted veins on the inner side of her left calf. By the end of a long shift on her feet the leg feels heavy and aches, and this eases when she rests with it raised. Foot pulses are normal and there is no redness, warmth or tenderness of the calf.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Acute deep vein thrombosis of the calf veins
options.B: Chronic peripheral arterial disease of the leg
options.C: Early cellulitis of the lower leg skin
options.D: Primary lymphoedema of the whole leg
options.E: Varicose veins from superficial venous reflux

correct_answer: E. Varicose veins from superficial venous reflux
why_correct: Visible, dilated, tortuous superficial veins with aching and heaviness that worsen after prolonged standing and ease with leg elevation are characteristic of varicose veins. They result from reflux through incompetent valves in the superficial veins. Referral to vascular services is for symptoms affecting quality of life or for complications such as skin changes, ulceration or bleeding. Source: NICE CKS, Varicose veins, 2024.
why_wrong: A. DVT causes acute pain, swelling and tenderness of the whole calf rather than visible superficial veins with standing-related aching. B. Peripheral arterial disease causes claudication and weak pulses and is relieved by dependency, not elevation. C. Cellulitis causes warmth, redness and tenderness. D. Lymphoedema causes swelling of the limb without prominent tortuous veins.
pearl: Heaviness and aching that build up with standing and ease with elevation, plus visible tortuous veins, point to varicose veins.
thinking: Visible tortuous superficial veins  ↓  Aching that worsens on standing and eases with elevation  ↓  No inflammation, normal pulses  ↓  Varicose veins
exam_trap: Choosing DVT because of calf symptoms without noting the chronic pattern and visible superficial veins.
takeaway: Tortuous superficial veins with standing-related heaviness are varicose veins.
notes: New occupational vignette. Near live S027/PAQ1093 test referral for treatment; this item tests recognition. CKS assessment wording checked (aching after standing, relief with elevation). Normal pulses added to rule out arterial disease.

stem:
A man in his thirties attends the emergency department with sudden severe pain from the loin to the groin and vomiting. He cannot lie still. He has no fever and is haemodynamically stable. Urine dipstick shows blood, with no nitrites or leucocytes.

Which mechanism best explains the blood in his urine?

options.A: Underlying urinary tract infection causing bleeding from the bladder lining
options.B: Abrasion of the urinary tract lining as the stone moves along it
options.C: Concentrated urine from dehydration irritating the bladder wall
options.D: Inflammation of the glomeruli triggered by the presence of the stone
options.E: A clotting disturbance brought on by severe pain and vomiting

correct_answer: B. Abrasion of the urinary tract lining as the stone moves along it
why_correct: A stone moving down the ureter scrapes and irritates the urothelium, so microscopic or visible haematuria is common in renal colic. The absence of nitrites and leucocytes makes infection an unlikely explanation. Source: NICE CKS, Renal or ureteric colic - acute, 2024.
why_wrong: A. A negative nitrite and leucocyte result argues against infection as the cause. C. Dehydration concentrates urine but does not itself make it bloody. D. A stone causes mechanical injury lower down, not glomerular disease. E. Pain and vomiting do not cause a bleeding tendency.
pearl: Haematuria is expected in renal colic, but its absence does not exclude a stone.
thinking: Loin-to-groin colic with dipstick blood  ↓  Stone is a sharp, moving mechanical irritant  ↓  Urothelium is scraped along the ureter  ↓  Haematuria from abrasion, not infection or glomerular disease
exam_trap: A, assuming blood in the urine means infection, but without nitrites, leucocytes or fever the stone itself is the more likely cause.
takeaway: Haematuria in renal colic comes from the stone abrading the urinary tract lining.
notes: New vignette (young man, dipstick negative for infection); same learning point as AKT N6673 (stone abrades urothelium). Key moved to B per plan. No source error found. Stem deliberately states nitrites and leucocytes negative so the infection distractor is excluded.
sources: https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/renal-or-ureteric-colic-acute/diagnosis/assessment/ (checked: haematuria common; dipstick for blood, nitrite, leucocyte esterase)
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng118 (opened; no dipstick or mechanism content)

stem:
A 62-year-old woman says that for several years she has leaked stool without warning, especially when hurrying to the toilet and sometimes when coughing. She sustained a third-degree perineal tear at her first delivery. Her bowel habit is otherwise regular, she is not constipated and she has no weight loss.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Faecal incontinence due to sphincter damage
options.B: Overflow diarrhoea secondary to faecal loading
options.C: Steatorrhoea from pancreatic exocrine failure
options.D: Bile acid diarrhoea after gallbladder removal
options.E: Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea

correct_answer: A. Faecal incontinence due to sphincter damage
why_correct: Involuntary loss of stool is faecal incontinence, and obstetric anal sphincter injury is a leading cause that can present years later. The regular habit and absence of constipation make overflow unlikely. Source: NICE CG49, Faecal incontinence in adults: management, 2007; NHS, Bowel incontinence.
why_wrong: B. Overflow occurs with constipation or impaction, which she does not have. C. Steatorrhoea gives pale, greasy, offensive stools rather than urgent or cough-related leakage. D. Bile acid diarrhoea follows gallbladder surgery, which is not described. E. IBS with diarrhoea causes pain-related altered habit, not sphincter-related leakage.
pearl: Previous obstetric anal sphincter injury is a key risk factor for faecal incontinence, which can appear decades later.
thinking: Leakage of stool without warning  ↓  Prior third-degree tear  ↓  Sphincter weakness is the likely mechanism  ↓  Faecal incontinence
exam_trap: B, overflow diarrhoea: only applies when constipation or impaction is present.
takeaway: Obstetric sphincter injury is a classic cause of faecal incontinence.
notes: New vignette; key at A as planned. NICE CG49 cited from knowledge, not re-fetched. Nearest live items are unrelated (urinary incontinence types etc.), so no duplicate.
sources: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/bowel-incontinence/ (checked: childbirth and weaker muscles as causes)

stem:
A 44-year-old woman has had her third renal stone in four years. Analysis of the latest stone shows it is made of calcium oxalate. Her serum calcium is normal. She asks which of her dietary habits might be contributing.

Which habit is most likely to increase her risk?

options.A: Drinking plenty of water spread evenly throughout the day
options.B: Keeping a normal dietary calcium intake from milk and cheese
options.C: Frequent large servings of spinach, rhubarb or nuts
options.D: Keeping salt intake below the recommended daily maximum
options.E: Adding fresh lemon juice to some of her daily drinks

correct_answer: C. Frequent large servings of spinach, rhubarb or nuts
why_correct: Oxalate-rich foods such as spinach, rhubarb and nuts raise urinary oxalate, which promotes calcium oxalate crystal formation. The other options are habits that are advised to reduce stone risk. Source: NHS, Kidney stones (prevention advice); Kidney Research UK, Kidney stones (reviewed October 2024).
why_wrong: A. Good hydration dilutes urine and lowers stone risk. B. Normal dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut and is protective, so restriction is not advised. D. Lower salt intake reduces urinary calcium. E. Citrate in lemon juice inhibits crystal formation.
pearl: Advise high fluid intake, normal calcium, modest salt and less oxalate-rich food; do not tell patients to cut calcium.
thinking: Recurrent calcium oxalate stones  ↓  Modifiable dietary contributors  ↓  Oxalate load raises urinary oxalate  ↓  Oxalate-rich foods increase risk; fluids, calcium, low salt protect
exam_trap: B, cutting calcium to cut calcium stones: dietary calcium lowers oxalate absorption, so restricting it can raise risk.
takeaway: Oxalate-rich foods raise calcium oxalate stone risk, whereas fluids, normal calcium and lower salt protect.
notes: AKT options were weak (e.g. 'vitamin C deficiency', 'never relevant'); rebuilt with protective-habit distractors. Key moved to C. NHS kidney stones page checked (fluids, enough calcium, salt limit); the oxalate and EAU statements are standard guidance, not re-fetched. NG118 does not cover diet.
sources: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/kidney-stones/ (checked: fluids, lemon juice, calcium, salt limit)

stem:
A 52-year-old man is on day two of an admission with gallstone pancreatitis. Despite initial intravenous fluids he becomes cold and clammy, his blood pressure falls markedly, his breathing becomes rapid and he is drowsy and disorientated.

Which complication should be suspected?

options.A: A pancreatic pseudocyst compressing the stomach
options.B: Gallstone ileus from a cholecystoenteric fistula
options.C: Splenic vein thrombosis with gastric varices
options.D: Chronic pancreatitis with steatorrhoea and weight loss
options.E: Systemic inflammation with early multi-organ failure

correct_answer: E. Systemic inflammation with early multi-organ failure
why_correct: Severe acute pancreatitis can trigger a systemic inflammatory response with shock, respiratory compromise and altered mental state, indicating developing organ failure. This needs urgent senior review and critical care assessment. Source: NICE NG104, Pancreatitis, 2018.
why_wrong: A. A pseudocyst forms weeks later and causes early satiety, not acute shock. B. Gallstone ileus is small bowel obstruction from an impacted stone, not an early feature of pancreatitis. C. Splenic vein thrombosis is a late local complication. D. Chronic pancreatitis is a long-term condition and does not explain acute collapse.
pearl: Hypotension, tachypnoea or confusion in acute pancreatitis means organ failure until proved otherwise.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis, now shocked and confused  ↓  Early deterioration over days, not weeks  ↓  Inflammatory cascade causes systemic illness  ↓  Suspect organ failure and escalate
exam_trap: A, pseudocyst: a classic named complication, but it develops over weeks and does not cause early shock.
takeaway: Hypotension and confusion in acute pancreatitis signal systemic inflammation with organ failure.
notes: New vignette with gallstone aetiology and time course; key moved to E. Distractors rewritten to be parallel. Nearest live item covers critical-care management, not recognising the complication. NG104 cited from knowledge, not re-fetched.

stem:
On the second evening after a hip hemiarthroplasty, a 79-year-old woman has an oxygen saturation of 89% on room air, a respiratory rate of 26 and new confusion. She received morphine this afternoon and has had intravenous fluids since surgery. Her early warning score is high.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Give oxygen, start an ABCDE assessment and call for senior help
options.B: Assume basal atelectasis and arrange chest physiotherapy alone
options.C: Start broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed hospital-acquired pneumonia
options.D: Give intravenous furosemide for presumed fluid overload
options.E: Reduce the oxygen to avoid suppressing her respiratory drive

correct_answer: A. Give oxygen, start an ABCDE assessment and call for senior help
why_correct: Postoperative hypoxia has many possible causes, including atelectasis, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolism and opioid-related hypoventilation, and the cause cannot be settled from the bedside picture alone. She needs oxygen titrated to a target saturation range, a structured ABCDE assessment and early senior review, as advised for acutely ill adults in hospital. Source: NICE CG50, Acutely ill adults in hospital, 2007; Royal College of Physicians, NEWS2, 2017; British Thoracic Society, guideline for oxygen use in healthcare and emergency settings, 2017.
why_wrong: B. Atelectasis is common, but assuming it and treating with physiotherapy alone risks missing pulmonary embolism or sepsis. C. Antibiotics alone treat only one possible cause and delay the assessment. D. Furosemide is unsafe if she is not fluid overloaded. E. A hypoxic patient with no known risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure needs oxygen titrated to the target range, not withheld.
pearl: In postoperative hypoxia, treat the hypoxia and look systematically for the cause rather than anchoring on one diagnosis.
thinking: Hypoxic and confused after surgery  ↓  Many possible causes, including opioids and embolism  ↓  Anchoring on one cause is dangerous  ↓  Oxygen, ABCDE assessment and early senior review
exam_trap: B, anchoring on atelectasis: it is the commonest cause but not the only one.
takeaway: Treat postoperative hypoxia with oxygen, a structured ABCDE assessment and early senior review, rather than fixing on one cause.
notes: New vignette (orthopaedic, older woman, opioid exposure); key at A per plan (AKT key was C). Option A includes oxygen so key is a complete first step. CG50 and BTS cited from knowledge, not re-fetched.

stem:
A 66-year-old woman returns to the surgical ward after an emergency laparotomy for a perforated diverticulum. A closed-suction drain has been left in the pelvis. Her family asks the trainee why it is there.

What is the main purpose of the drain?

options.A: To show that no anastomotic leak has occurred
options.B: To allow blood, pus or other fluid to escape from the area
options.C: To replace the need for postoperative antibiotics
options.D: To reduce the risk of venous thrombosis in the legs after surgery
options.E: To prevent infection of the surgical wound

correct_answer: B. To allow blood, pus or other fluid to escape from the area
why_correct: Drains are used selectively to let blood, pus or other fluid collections escape from the operative site and can alert the team to bleeding or a leak. They do not prevent complications and do not replace antibiotics or thromboprophylaxis. Source: ERAS Society recommendations for perioperative care in colorectal surgery (2025 update).
why_wrong: A. A drain cannot confirm that an anastomosis is intact, and a clear output does not exclude a leak. C. Drains do not treat or prevent infection and never replace antibiotics. D. Thromboprophylaxis uses mechanical measures and low molecular weight heparin. E. Drains do not prevent wound infection and can themselves be a route for infection.
pearl: Drains remove collections and may give early warning of bleeding or leak, but they are not routine after most operations.
thinking: Drain left after laparotomy  ↓  What can a drain actually do  ↓  Removes fluid collections  ↓  Drainage of fluid from operative site

A 74-year-old woman with an end colostomy formed two years ago presents with a bulge beside her stoma that has become very painful over a day. She has vomited several times and has not passed any stool or gas into her bag. The swelling is firm and tender and can no longer be pushed back.

What complication is most likely?

options.A: Irritant dermatitis from leakage onto the surrounding skin
options.B: Strangulated bowel within the parastomal hernia
options.C: A simple, uncomplicated parastomal hernia
options.D: Separation of the stoma from the skin edge
options.E: Pyoderma gangrenosum around the stoma

correct_answer: B. Strangulated bowel within the parastomal hernia
why_correct: Constant pain, vomiting, absent output and a hernia that cannot be reduced indicate that bowel is trapped and may have lost its blood supply. This needs emergency surgical assessment. Source: NHS, Colostomy: complications (urgent help for obstruction symptoms), and European Hernia Society guidelines on prevention and treatment of parastomal hernias, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Dermatitis causes sore skin, not vomiting or an irreducible lump. C. An uncomplicated hernia is soft and reducible and does not cause obstruction symptoms. D. Separation at the skin edge shows a gap at the stoma margin and does not cause an irreducible tender swelling with obstruction. E. Pyoderma gangrenosum is a painful ulcer of the skin, not a firm swelling with vomiting.
pearl: A painful, tense, irreducible parastomal hernia with vomiting and no output is incarcerated or strangulated until proved otherwise.
thinking: Parastomal bulge  ↓  Now painful, irreducible, vomiting, no output  ↓  Obstruction with possible strangulation  ↓  Emergency surgical review
exam_trap: Reassuring a patient about a long-standing hernia can miss the point at which it has become irreducible.
takeaway: A painful irreducible hernia with vomiting needs emergency surgical assessment.

A 34-year-old man has had a foul-smelling discharge from his left ear on and off for over a year, with gradually worsening hearing in that ear. Otoscopy shows a retraction pocket in the upper part of the eardrum with white flaky debris. He asks why he is being referred to ENT rather than simply given ear drops.

Why is this condition important?

options.A: It is caused by a build-up of ordinary earwax
options.B: It causes a short-lived blockage that clears by itself
options.C: It is a disorder of the retina
options.D: It can erode adjacent bone and ear structures
options.E: It resolves with a short course of ear drops

correct_answer: D. It can erode adjacent bone and ear structures
why_correct: The picture is of cholesteatoma, a collection of keratinising skin in the middle ear that expands slowly. It can destroy the ossicles, damage the facial nerve or inner ear and spread to the brain, so surgical management is usually needed. Source: NHS, Cholesteatoma, and NICE CKS, Otitis media - chronic suppurative (referral to ENT).
why_wrong: A. Cholesteatoma is not simple wax, and wax does not erode bone. B. It does not clear by itself, and a temporary blockage would not explain the destructive course. C. Cholesteatoma affects the ear, not the retina. E. Ear drops may reduce discharge for a time but do not remove the keratin collection, so surgery is usually needed.
pearl: Persistent foul discharge with hearing loss and an attic retraction pocket should prompt ENT referral because cholesteatoma erodes bone.
thinking: Chronic foul ear discharge with hearing loss  ↓  Attic retraction pocket with debris  ↓  Cholesteatoma  ↓  ENT referral because it erodes structures
exam_trap: Treating with repeated ear drops alone allows silent bone erosion.
takeaway: Cholesteatoma matters because it destroys surrounding structures and needs ENT care.
notes: Source was a bare recall question; a short vignette was built around the same fact.

A 77-year-old woman with a mechanical heart valve takes warfarin. She presents with a nosebleed that has continued for 40 minutes despite firm pinching of the soft part of her nose. Her pulse and blood pressure are normal.

Which investigation is most important to arrange now?

options.A: Serum amylase
options.B: Peak expiratory flow rate
options.C: INR blood test
options.D: Fasting HbA1c
options.E: Visual acuity

correct_answer: C. INR blood test
why_correct: Warfarin can prolong bleeding, and the degree of anticoagulation guides further management. An urgent INR (with a full blood count) shows whether reversal or other action is needed alongside local measures. Source: NICE CKS, Epistaxis (nosebleeds), which lists coagulation studies for people taking warfarin and immediate transfer to A&E when bleeding persists after 10 to 15 minutes of pressure; NHS, Nosebleed.
why_wrong: A. Amylase is for suspected pancreatitis and does not help with a nosebleed. B. Peak flow assesses asthma and is unrelated to this bleed. D. HbA1c reflects long-term glucose control and does not guide management of acute bleeding on warfarin. E. Visual acuity is not relevant to a nosebleed on anticoagulation.
pearl: In any bleeding patient on warfarin, check the INR urgently; reversal depends on severity of bleeding and INR.
thinking: Epistaxis on warfarin  ↓  Local pressure first  ↓  Check INR and full blood count  ↓  Escalate to reversal if serious bleeding
exam_trap: Treating only the nose and forgetting the anticoagulant status.
takeaway: Check the INR urgently in anyone bleeding on warfarin.
notes: Options reworded to remove the 'only' cue; same key as source.

A 71-year-old former smoker has an abdominal ultrasound for abnormal liver tests. It incidentally shows a small infrarenal aortic aneurysm. He has no abdominal or back pain and is haemodynamically stable. He asks what happens next.

What is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Emergency transfer to theatre for open repair
options.B: Discharge with no follow-up as the aneurysm is small
options.C: Ultrasound surveillance with risk-factor control
options.D: Arrange urgent CT mesenteric angiography
options.E: Immediate admission for blood transfusion

correct_answer: C. Ultrasound surveillance with risk-factor control
why_correct: This is an asymptomatic small abdominal aortic aneurysm. It is managed by regular ultrasound surveillance within a vascular service, together with addressing smoking, blood pressure and lipids. Repair is considered if it enlarges, becomes symptomatic or reaches a larger size. Source: NICE NG156, Abdominal aortic aneurysm: diagnosis and management, 2020.
why_wrong: A. Emergency repair is for a ruptured or symptomatic aneurysm, not a small incidental finding. B. Small aneurysms can still grow, so discharge without follow-up would miss a later need for repair. D. There is no pain or feature of mesenteric ischaemia, so urgent angiography is not required. E. He is stable with no bleeding, so transfusion and admission are not needed.
pearl: Small asymptomatic AAAs are watched with ultrasound surveillance and cardiovascular risk reduction; symptoms or growth prompt assessment for repair.
thinking: Incidental small AAA  ↓  No pain, stable  ↓  Not a rupture  ↓  Surveillance ultrasound plus risk-factor control
exam_trap: Over-treating an incidental finding, or discharging it without surveillance.
takeaway: Small asymptomatic aneurysms need surveillance and risk reduction, not emergency surgery.
notes: Source asked for a diagnosis from a description (thin item). Re-angled to management of an asymptomatic small AAA, with no size threshold tested.

A 52-year-old woman receives an NHS invitation to breast screening and asks her GP what it is for. She has no symptoms and no family history. Her friend believes screening means she will never get breast cancer, and that she would not need to report a lump found between appointments.

What best describes the purpose of the programme?

options.A: To prevent breast cancer from ever developing
options.B: To make a diagnosis in every woman with a benign breast lump
options.C: To find breast cancer early in women without symptoms
options.D: To replace clinical assessment of lumps found between screens
options.E: To screen for ovarian cancer at the same visit

correct_answer: C. To find breast cancer early in women without symptoms
why_correct: Mammographic screening looks for cancer in women who feel well, aiming to detect it early when treatment is more effective. It does not prevent cancer and does not replace assessment of new symptoms, so a woman who finds a lump should seek review at once. Source: NHS England, NHS Breast Screening Programme guidance, current.
why_wrong: A. Screening cannot prevent cancer, only detect it earlier. B. Screening is not used to diagnose benign lumps; symptomatic women are assessed through a diagnostic service. D. A symptomatic lump always needs referral irrespective of recent screening, so screening cannot replace assessment. E. The programme examines the breasts only and does not screen for ovarian cancer.
pearl: Population screening aims for earlier detection in asymptomatic women; symptoms always need separate assessment.
thinking: Well woman invited to screening  ↓  Screening finds disease before symptoms  ↓  Aim is earlier detection  ↓  New lump still needs referral
exam_trap: Assuming a recent normal screen excludes cancer in a woman with a new lump.
takeaway: Screening detects cancer early but does not prevent it or replace assessment of symptoms.

A 68-year-old man had a total hip replacement under spinal anaesthesia 12 hours ago and is receiving regular opioid analgesia. He now complains of lower abdominal discomfort and has passed only a small dribble of urine over several hours. He is afebrile and his observations are stable.

What is the most appropriate initial assessment?

options.A: Start empirical antibiotics for a urinary tract infection
options.B: Encourage extra oral fluids for dehydration
options.C: Give a laxative for constipation
options.D: Stop the intravenous fluids to reduce urine volume
options.E: Examine the lower abdomen and perform a bladder scan

correct_answer: E. Examine the lower abdomen and perform a bladder scan
why_correct: Spinal anaesthesia, opioids and immobility make postoperative urinary retention likely. A bladder scan confirms a large residual volume and shows whether catheterisation is needed. Source: NICE CKS, Lower urinary tract symptoms in men (urinary retention scenario).
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not indicated without features of infection and would not relieve a retained bladder. B. Extra oral fluids would fill the bladder further if it is already retained. C. A laxative addresses constipation, not suprapubic discomfort with minimal urine output. D. Stopping fluids does not treat retention and risks hypovolaemia after surgery.
pearl: After anaesthesia and opioids, think retention in any patient who cannot void; confirm with a bladder scan before catheterising.
thinking: Cannot pass urine after surgery  ↓  Spinal anaesthesia and opioids  ↓  Suspect retention  ↓  Bladder scan, then catheterise if needed
exam_trap: Assuming low output means dehydration and giving fluids rather than checking the bladder.
takeaway: Think retention when a postoperative patient cannot pass urine.
notes: A live item on postoperative acute urinary retention exists but tests the diagnosis; this one tests the first assessment step.

A woman in her seventies with a history of pelvic surgery has colicky pain, bloating and repeated vomiting. Her CT report describes a 'transition point' in the ileum.

How should this finding be interpreted?

options.A: The normal junction between the small and large bowel
options.B: A segment of bowel wall thickened by inflammation
options.C: An area of free perforation with gas outside the bowel
options.D: Dilated bowel upstream, collapsed bowel downstream
options.E: Generalised ileus with no site of blockage

correct_answer: D. Dilated bowel upstream, collapsed bowel downstream
why_correct: A transition point is where dilated bowel above meets decompressed bowel below. It confirms mechanical obstruction and points to its site, commonly an adhesion from previous pelvic surgery or a hernia. Source: standard CT interpretation of small bowel obstruction (Radiopaedia, Small bowel obstruction).
why_wrong: A. The ileocaecal valve is a normal landmark and not what a transition point describes. B. Thickening of the wall suggests inflammation, which is a different finding. C. Free gas outside the bowel indicates perforation, which is different from a change in calibre. E. In ileus the bowel is dilated throughout, with no change in calibre at a particular point.
pearl: A transition point on CT shows mechanical obstruction and localises the cause; adhesions are commonest after previous abdominal surgery.
thinking: Vomiting, distension and colic  ↓  CT shows a change in calibre  ↓  Transition point  ↓  Mechanical obstruction with a site to find the cause
exam_trap: Confusing a calibre change with wall thickening or ileus.
takeaway: A transition point is where dilated bowel meets collapsed bowel.
notes: Adapted; clinical content verified against established UK guidance, no source error found.

A 60-year-old man had a colostomy formed two weeks ago. A nurse teaches him how to check his stoma at each bag change, and he asks what a healthy stoma should look like.

Which description fits a healthy stoma?

options.A: Pink to red and moist
options.B: Dark blue-grey
options.C: Black
options.D: Pale yellow with a dry surface
options.E: White and shrunken

correct_answer: A. Pink to red and moist
why_correct: A well-perfused stoma is moist and pink to red, like the inside of the mouth. Dusky, blue, grey or black colour suggests poor blood supply and needs urgent surgical review. Source: Association of Stoma Care Nurses UK, Stoma care guidelines, current.
why_wrong: B. Dark blue-grey suggests venous congestion or ischaemia and needs review. C. Black indicates necrosis and needs urgent surgical review. D. A pale yellow dry stoma is not the normal appearance and suggests an unhealthy mucosa. E. White and shrunken mucosa suggests poor perfusion.
pearl: A healthy stoma is moist and pink to red; dusky, blue-grey or black means ischaemia.
thinking: Fresh stoma  ↓  Look at colour and moisture  ↓  Moist pink or red is healthy  ↓  Dusky or black needs urgent review
exam_trap: Dismissing a dark stoma as normal bruising.
takeaway: A healthy stoma is moist and pink to red.

A 47-year-old woman reports that over three weeks her left breast has become larger, warm and red over much of its surface, and the skin looks like orange peel. She is not breastfeeding and has no fever. A week of oral antibiotics from her GP has made no difference.

Which diagnosis must be considered?

options.A: Widespread fibrocystic change
options.B: Galactocele
options.C: Inflammatory breast cancer
options.D: Lactational mastitis
options.E: Giant fibroadenoma

correct_answer: C. Inflammatory breast cancer
why_correct: Rapid diffuse redness, swelling and peau d'orange outside lactation and without response to antibiotics should prompt suspicion of inflammatory breast cancer. NICE advises considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for skin changes that suggest breast cancer, and she needs urgent breast assessment. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Fibrocystic change is usually cyclical and does not cause rapid redness and skin dimpling. B. A galactocele is a milk-filled cyst in lactation and is not warm, red and diffuse. D. Lactational mastitis occurs during breastfeeding and usually settles with antibiotics. E. A giant fibroadenoma is a discrete mass, mainly in young women, and does not cause diffuse skin redness.
pearl: Inflammatory breast cancer mimics mastitis; suspect it when there is no lactation or no response to antibiotics.
thinking: Red, swollen breast with orange-peel skin  ↓  Not lactating, no response to antibiotics  ↓  Inflammatory breast cancer  ↓  Suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: Giving a second course of antibiotics for presumed infection.
takeaway: A red breast that fails to respond to antibiotics may be cancer.

A 19-year-old man is seen two days after being hit on the nose during a football match. His nose looks straight but he cannot breathe through either side. Anterior rhinoscopy shows a red, bulging, soft swelling on both sides of the septum.

Why does this finding need prompt drainage?

options.A: It commonly leads to leakage of cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: It permanently destroys the sense of smell
options.C: It starves the cartilage of blood and can collapse the nose
options.D: It blocks the Eustachian tube and often leads to middle ear disease
options.E: It signals an underlying bleeding disorder

correct_answer: C. It starves the cartilage of blood and can collapse the nose
why_correct: A septal haematoma lifts the perichondrium off the cartilage, which depends on it for its blood supply. Left undrained, it can cause cartilage necrosis, abscess formation and collapse of the nasal bridge. Source: NHS, Broken nose, and standard ENT management of septal haematoma (urgent drainage).
why_wrong: A. CSF leak follows skull base fracture, not a septal haematoma. B. Smell is not usually permanently lost, and that is not why drainage is needed. D. Nasal blockage does not reliably cause Eustachian tube dysfunction, and that is not the reason for urgent drainage. E. A septal haematoma follows local trauma and does not signal a bleeding disorder; the urgency is to protect the cartilage.
pearl: After nasal trauma, look inside for a boggy septum; treat a septal haematoma by prompt drainage to protect the cartilage.
thinking: Blunt nasal trauma with blocked nose  ↓  Bilateral boggy septal swelling  ↓  Septal haematoma  ↓  Urgent drainage to prevent cartilage necrosis
exam_trap: Assuming a straight nose means there is no injury needing treatment.
takeaway: A septal haematoma needs prompt drainage to prevent cartilage loss.
notes: Adapted; clinical content verified against established UK guidance, no source error found.

A 63-year-old man had a sigmoid colon cancer resected a year ago. Follow-up CT now shows several rounded lesions scattered through both lobes of the liver, and his liver enzymes are mildly raised.

Through which route does colorectal cancer most commonly reach the liver?

options.A: Spread through the cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: Spread via the portal venous system
options.C: Spread along the coronary arteries
options.D: Spread through the thoracic duct
options.E: Spread through the lungs

correct_answer: B. Spread via the portal venous system
why_correct: Veins from the large bowel drain into the portal vein and on to the liver, so tumour cells commonly seed there first. The liver is therefore the commonest site for distant spread of colorectal cancer. Source: NICE NG151, Colorectal cancer (management of colorectal liver metastases, section 1.5), and standard anatomy of the portal venous drainage.
why_wrong: A. Cerebrospinal fluid is not a route to the liver. C. Coronary arteries supply the heart and do not carry tumour cells from bowel to liver. D. The thoracic duct drains lymph to the left subclavian vein and is not the usual route to the liver. E. The lungs are not on the route to the liver; blood from the bowel passes through the portal system first.
pearl: Colorectal cancer metastasises to the liver via the portal vein, the commonest site of distant disease.
thinking: Bowel cancer  ↓  Venous drainage via the portal vein  ↓  Liver is the first capillary bed  ↓  Liver metastases
exam_trap: Choosing lymphatic spread because it sounds typical of cancer.
takeaway: The portal vein carries colorectal cancer to the liver.
notes: Adapted; clinical content verified against established UK guidance, no source error found.

A 38-year-old woman who recently finished a long-haul flight notices a hard, tender, red line running along the inner side of her calf over a varicose vein. She has no chest symptoms. The rest of the leg is not swollen and the foot is warm with normal pulses.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Gout
options.B: Cellulitis spreading across the lower leg
options.C: Acute arterial occlusion
options.D: Chronic osteomyelitis
options.E: Superficial vein thrombophlebitis

correct_answer: E. Superficial vein thrombophlebitis
why_correct: A tender, red cord along a superficial vein indicates thrombus and inflammation in that vein. Ultrasound may be needed to look for extension towards the deep system or a coexisting deep vein thrombosis, particularly after a long flight. Arterial occlusion produces a cold, pale, painful limb with absent pulses. D. Chronic osteomyelitis causes deep bone pain and sinus formation, not a superficial cord.
pearl: A tender red cord along a superficial vein is thrombophlebitis; consider ultrasound for extension or coexisting DVT.
thinking: Red, tender cord along a vein  ↓  Warm foot, pulses present  ↓  Superficial thrombophlebitis  ↓  Consider ultrasound for DVT
exam_trap: Missing a coexisting deep vein thrombosis.
takeaway: A tender cord along a superficial vein is thrombophlebitis.

A 13-year-old boy attends with a day of lower abdominal pain and vomiting. He was kicked in the groin during sport yesterday, and his mother thinks it is a bruise. On examination the right testis is exquisitely tender, lies transversely and is higher than the left. He has no fever or urinary symptoms.

What is the priority?

options.A: Refer for urgent surgical exploration, treating this as torsion
options.B: Arrange a Doppler ultrasound and wait for the result
options.C: Treat as epididymo-orchitis with antibiotics and review in two days
options.D: Give analgesia and see him again if pain persists
options.E: Diagnose a torted appendage and manage with rest

correct_answer: A. Refer for urgent surgical exploration, treating this as torsion
why_correct: A high, horizontal, very tender testis in an adolescent suggests testicular torsion, and recent minor trauma does not exclude it. He needs urgent surgical exploration, because delay risks losing the testis. Source: NICE CKS, Scrotal pain, and BAUS guidance, current.
why_wrong: B. Waiting for imaging delays treatment and should not hold up exploration when torsion is likely. C. Epididymo-orchitis is uncommon at this age and does not fit a high horizontal testis without fever or urinary features. D. Analgesia and later review risk testicular loss while the problem goes untreated. E. A torted appendage is usually confirmed at surgery or by a blue dot sign, and assuming it is unsafe.
pearl: In adolescent boys, a high tender testis with abdominal pain is torsion until proved otherwise, even after minor trauma.
thinking: Boy with abdominal pain and vomiting  ↓  High, horizontal tender testis  ↓  Torsion until proved otherwise  ↓  Urgent surgical exploration
exam_trap: Attributing the pain to trauma and not examining the testes.
takeaway: Always examine the testes in a boy with abdominal pain; suspected torsion means urgent exploration.

An 83-year-old woman in a care home has become agitated and has not passed urine since yesterday. She has had constipation for a week, takes oxybutynin for urgency and has a tender, palpable suprapubic mass. Her temperature is normal.

What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Increase her oral fluids and recheck the bladder later today
options.B: Start a laxative and see if urine is passed once her bowels open
options.C: Catheterise now and then look for reversible causes
options.D: Add an alpha-blocker and refer routinely to urology
options.E: Review in the continence clinic next month

correct_answer: C. Catheterise now and then look for reversible causes
why_correct: She has acute urinary retention, probably from constipation and an anticholinergic drug. Catheterisation relieves the retention, then constipation, medicines and renal function are reviewed. Source: NICE CKS, Urinary retention - acute, current.
why_wrong: A. More fluids would fill an already retained bladder. B. A laxative may help later but does not relieve a painful full bladder now. D. An alpha-blocker is mainly for male prostatic obstruction, and routine referral delays drainage. E. A review next month leaves her retained and at risk of kidney injury and delirium.
pearl: Acute retention needs urgent catheterisation, then a search for causes such as constipation, anticholinergic drugs or prostatic enlargement.
thinking: Confused older patient, palpable bladder  ↓  Acute urinary retention  ↓  Catheterise  ↓  Review constipation, drugs, renal function
exam_trap: Treating the cause first while the bladder stays full.
takeaway: Drain first, then find the cause of retention.

A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation develops sudden, severe pain in her right foot over one hour. The foot looks pale and feels cold to touch.

Which examination finding would most strongly support an acute arterial occlusion?

options.A: Bounding pedal pulses with a warm, well-perfused foot
options.B: Brisk capillary refill in every toe of the affected foot
options.C: Prominent varicose veins with brown skin staining at the shin
options.D: Pitting oedema of the whole leg with a normal temperature
options.E: Absent pulses in the foot with delayed capillary refill

correct_answer: E. Absent pulses in the foot with delayed capillary refill
why_correct: A sudden pale, cold, painful limb with absent distal pulses and delayed capillary refill indicates that an embolus or thrombus has blocked arterial inflow. Atrial fibrillation is a typical source of embolus. This is limb-threatening and needs same-day vascular assessment. Source: NICE CKS Peripheral arterial disease and Vascular Society acute limb ischaemia guidance (UK).
why_wrong: A. Bounding pulses and a warm foot indicate intact arterial flow, which is the opposite of occlusion. B. Brisk capillary refill indicates preserved perfusion. C. Varicose veins and staining reflect chronic venous disease, not sudden arterial loss. D. Pitting oedema with normal temperature suggests a venous or systemic cause such as venous insufficiency or heart failure.
pearl: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia and paralysis describe an acutely ischaemic limb; the later features (sensory loss, weakness) mark a threatened limb.
thinking: Sudden painful pale cold foot  ↓  Atrial fibrillation gives an embolic source  ↓  Arterial inflow is blocked  ↓  Distal pulses absent with poor capillary refill
exam_trap: Do not wait for imaging: absent pulses plus sensory or motor change means urgent vascular referral.
takeaway: A cold, pale, pulseless limb of sudden onset is acute limb ischaemia until proven otherwise.
notes: Source question was a one-line recall item; built a vignette around the same fact (absent distal pulse). Live PLAB items cover ALI management/imaging, not the examination finding. No clinical error found in the source. Sources reflect standard UK guidance relied on; not re-fetched this session.
sources: NICE CKS Peripheral arterial disease (relied on, not re-fetched)
Vascular Society acute limb ischaemia guidance (relied on, not re-fetched)

stem:
A 62-year-old man returns to the surgical ward after an anterior resection. Four hours later he looks pale and clammy with a heart rate of 128 beats/min and a blood pressure of 82/50 mmHg. His abdomen is becoming distended and the pelvic drain has filled with fresh blood over the past hour.

Which complication should be suspected first?

options.A: Anastomotic leak with early faecal peritonitis
options.B: Reactionary haemorrhage from the operative site
options.C: Paralytic ileus with fluid loss into the bowel
options.D: Massive pulmonary embolism from deep vein thrombosis
options.E: Epidural-related hypotension from a high block

correct_answer: B. Reactionary haemorrhage from the operative site
why_correct: Early shock with rising drain output of fresh blood shortly after surgery indicates reactionary haemorrhage from the operative site. It needs immediate resuscitation with an ABCDE approach, blood and senior surgical review for return to theatre. Source: NICE CG50, Acutely ill adults in hospital: recognising and responding to deterioration, and standard UK surgical teaching on reactionary haemorrhage.
why_wrong: A. An anastomotic leak typically presents several days after surgery with fever and peritonitis, not fresh blood in the drain within hours. C. Ileus causes distension and vomiting but not haemorrhagic shock. D. Pulmonary embolism causes breathlessness and chest pain, with no blood in the drain. E. Epidural hypotension would not explain fresh blood in the drain or the distension.
pearl: Early postoperative shock with fresh blood in a drain means bleeding until proven otherwise; a falling drain output can also be false reassurance if the drain has blocked.
thinking: Early post-op tachycardia and hypotension  ↓  Fresh blood filling the drain  ↓  Haemorrhagic shock  ↓  Reactionary haemorrhage: resuscitate and call senior surgeon
exam_trap: Attributing early post-operative hypotension to dehydration or analgesia delays the return to theatre.
takeaway: Hypotension, tachycardia and increasing bloody drain output soon after surgery is haemorrhage until proven otherwise.
notes: Original was a one-line recall item; built a vignette. No clinical error found in the source. Near live items cover DVT/PE/drain blockage, not post-operative haemorrhage. Standard teaching, not re-fetched.
sources: RCS England postoperative care / Good Surgical Practice (relied on, not re-fetched)

stem:
A 55-year-old woman develops noisy, laboured breathing in recovery shortly after a total thyroidectomy. She has audible inspiratory stridor and a weak, breathy voice, and laryngoscopy shows both vocal cords lying close to the midline.

What is the most immediate danger to her?

options.A: Acute upper airway obstruction
options.B: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany
options.C: Aspiration pneumonia developing next week
options.D: Permanent hoarseness affecting her work
options.E: Thyrotoxic crisis from released hormone

correct_answer: A. Acute upper airway obstruction
why_correct: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury leaves both cords near the midline, which narrows the glottic airway and produces stridor. The immediate threat is complete airway obstruction, so senior anaesthetic and ENT help, oxygen and preparation for airway rescue are needed. Source: ENT UK and BAETS guidance on thyroid surgery complications.
why_wrong: B. Hypocalcaemia is a recognised complication but develops over days and does not cause stridor from cord position. C. Aspiration is a later risk and is not the immediate threat. D. Voice outcome matters, but it is secondary to securing the airway. E. Thyroid storm is rare and does not cause midline vocal cord position.
pearl: Stridor with bilateral cord palsy after neck surgery is an airway emergency; unilateral palsy usually causes a hoarse voice rather than stridor.
thinking: Stridor after thyroid surgery  ↓  Both cords at the midline  ↓  Glottic airway narrowed  ↓  Airway obstruction is the immediate danger
exam_trap: Stridor is not a voice problem: treat the airway first, then deal with voice and calcium.
takeaway: Bilateral vocal cord palsy after neck surgery threatens the airway immediately.
notes: Source stem was a one-line item; rebuilt as a post-thyroidectomy scenario with a laryngoscopy finding. No clinical error found. Near live items are other airway emergencies, not this scenario. Standard teaching, not re-fetched.
sources: ENT UK / BAETS thyroid surgery guidance (relied on, not re-fetched)

presentation: Persistent throat pain in a smoker
stem:
A 66-year-old man who has smoked for 45 years and drinks alcohol heavily has had a one-sided sore throat for three months. The pain is referred to his right ear and he feels food sticking in his throat. His ear examination is normal.

Which diagnosis is most important to exclude?

options.A: Chronic Eustachian tube dysfunction from allergy
options.B: Recurrent streptococcal tonsillitis
options.C: Laryngopharyngeal reflux disease alone
options.D: Squamous cell cancer of the head and neck
options.E: Temporomandibular joint dysfunction

correct_answer: D. Squamous cell cancer of the head and neck
why_correct: Persistent unilateral throat pain with referred otalgia and dysphagia in a heavy smoker and drinker is a red-flag combination for head and neck cancer. Referred ear pain with a normal ear examination suggests a pharyngeal or laryngeal source. Dysphagia alone warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12, section 1.2), so he needs urgent assessment through that pathway rather than treatment for a benign cause. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026), sections 1.2 and 1.8.
why_wrong: A. Eustachian tube dysfunction causes ear fullness and does not explain persistent unilateral throat pain with dysphagia. B. Recurrent tonsillitis is episodic and febrile rather than a three-month unilateral problem. C. Reflux is a diagnosis of exclusion and should not be assumed when red-flag features are present. E. Temporomandibular disorder causes jaw and ear pain but not dysphagia with a unilateral sore throat.
pearl: Persistent unilateral sore throat with referred ear pain and dysphagia in a smoker is cancer until proved otherwise; dysphagia at any age warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral.
thinking: Older smoker and heavy drinker  ↓  Unilateral persistent throat pain with referred otalgia and dysphagia  ↓  Normal ear examination, so source is pharyngeal or laryngeal  ↓  Consider head and neck cancer
exam_trap: A normal ear examination with ear pain does not exclude serious disease: the pain is referred from the throat.
takeaway: Persistent unilateral throat symptoms with dysphagia in a smoker mean head and neck cancer until excluded.
notes: Source stem (dysphagia, sore throat, smoker) adapted with unilateral pain and referred otalgia; wording uses 'suspected cancer pathway referral' with no day count. Oesophageal-cancer items are live, but none test head and neck cancer. NG12 not re-fetched this session.
sources: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (relied on, not re-fetched)

stem:
A 58-year-old woman notices a firm lump in her left breast. The overlying skin is thickened and dimpled with closely spaced small pits, and the skin looks swollen.

Which term describes this skin change?

options.A: Erythema nodosum
options.B: Peau d'orange
options.C: Paget change of the nipple
options.D: Livedo reticularis
options.E: Cutis laxa

correct_answer: B. Peau d'orange
why_correct: Peau d'orange is thickened, dimpled skin caused by oedema when a tumour blocks the dermal lymphatics. It suggests locally advanced or inflammatory breast cancer. She needs urgent suspected cancer pathway referral for triple assessment. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Erythema nodosum is tender red nodules on the shins. C. Paget change is an eczematous change of the nipple and areola, not skin dimpling over a lump. D. Livedo reticularis is a mottled lace-like purple pattern of the limbs. E. Cutis laxa is a rare inherited disorder with loose, sagging skin.
pearl: Skin changes such as peau d'orange, dimpling or nipple retraction with a lump are red flags for breast cancer.
thinking: Breast lump with swollen dimpled skin  ↓  Lymphatic obstruction causes skin oedema  ↓  This is peau d'orange  ↓  Suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: Do not label skin thickening over a breast lump as infection and give antibiotics alone.
takeaway: Peau d'orange over a breast lump suggests cancer blocking the dermal lymphatics.
notes: Source described the lesion as 'resembling an orange peel', which cues the answer; stem now describes dimpling without the cue. Live breast items cover referral, not this sign. Standard teaching, not re-fetched.
sources: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (relied on, not re-fetched)

stem:
A 49-year-old woman has been diagnosed with carcinoma of the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. On examination she now has firm, palpable nodes in her right axilla.

What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Benign reactive nodes needing no further assessment
options.B: Proof of established distant metastatic disease
options.C: Spread to the regional draining nodes
options.D: Unrelated lymphadenopathy from a recent viral infection
options.E: Lymphoedema caused by an axillary vein thrombosis

correct_answer: C. Spread to the regional draining nodes
why_correct: The axillary nodes are the first draining station of the breast, so enlarged ipsilateral nodes most likely reflect regional lymphatic spread. This affects staging and prognosis and is usually confirmed with axillary ultrasound and biopsy or sentinel node assessment. Source: NICE NG101 Early and locally advanced breast cancer (UK).
why_wrong: A. Nodes in a known breast cancer should be assessed and not assumed reactive. B. Axillary involvement is regional spread, not by itself distant metastasis. D. An unrelated viral cause is unlikely when the nodes are firm and on the same side as the cancer. E. Venous thrombosis causes arm swelling rather than discrete firm nodes.
pearl: Axillary node status is a major prognostic factor in breast cancer and guides further treatment.
thinking: Known breast cancer  ↓  Firm ipsilateral axillary nodes  ↓  Axilla is the first draining station  ↓  Regional lymphatic spread
exam_trap: Regional node spread is not the same as distant metastasis; do not mix up staging categories.
takeaway: New ipsilateral axillary nodes in breast cancer indicate regional lymphatic spread.
notes: Source key 'potentially' regional spread; kept the 'most likely' wording and added the need for assessment. Live axillary items are abscess/lymphoma, not this point. NG101 not re-fetched.
sources: NICE NG101 Early and locally advanced breast cancer (relied on, not re-fetched)

stem:
A 38-year-old man develops sudden severe spinning vertigo with nausea after a recent cold. It has lasted two days. He also reports muffled hearing and ringing in his left ear since the onset, and has never had a similar episode. He has no vascular risk factors, limb weakness, speech disturbance or double vision, and examination shows horizontal nystagmus.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Viral labyrinthitis
options.B: Vestibular neuritis
options.C: Ménière disease
options.D: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
options.E: Posterior circulation stroke

correct_answer: A. Viral labyrinthitis
why_correct: Acute prolonged vertigo with new hearing loss or tinnitus points to labyrinthitis, in which both the vestibular and cochlear parts of the inner ear are inflamed, often after a viral illness. Absent central neurological signs and vascular risk factors make a central cause less likely. Source: NICE CKS Vertigo, and NHS, Labyrinthitis and vestibular neuritis.
why_wrong: B. Vestibular neuritis causes prolonged vertigo without hearing loss or tinnitus. C. Ménière disease causes recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting hours with fluctuating hearing loss, not a first episode. D. BPPV causes brief positional spells lasting under a minute with normal hearing. E. A central cause is less likely without other brainstem or cerebellar signs, though it must stay in mind in high-risk patients.
pearl: Acute vertigo with hearing loss or tinnitus suggests labyrinthitis; the same picture without hearing loss is vestibular neuritis. New one-sided hearing loss still needs prompt assessment.
thinking: Acute prolonged vertigo  ↓  Hearing loss and tinnitus present  ↓  Inner ear (cochlea and vestibule) involved  ↓  Labyrinthitis
exam_trap: Missing the hearing change and choosing vestibular neuritis, or forgetting to exclude central signs.
takeaway: Prolonged acute vertigo with hearing loss is labyrinthitis.
notes: Source options included otitis externa; replaced with a safer central-cause distractor. Key and logic unchanged. Live vertigo items cover neuritis, BPPV, Ménière; none test labyrinthitis. Standard teaching, not re-fetched.
sources: NICE CKS Vertigo / Dizziness (relied on, not re-fetched)

presentation: Persistent pelvic pain in a man
stem:
A 41-year-old man has had five months of aching discomfort in the perineum and above the pubis, with urinary frequency and pain on ejaculation. He has had no fever or loin pain, his urine dipstick and culture are negative, and he is otherwise well.

Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.A: Acute epididymo-orchitis
options.B: Chronic prostatitis
options.C: Acute bacterial prostatitis
options.D: Benign prostatic enlargement
options.E: Bladder calculus

correct_answer: B. Chronic prostatitis
why_correct: Months of pelvic or perineal pain with urinary symptoms and pain on ejaculation, without fever or infection on urine testing, is typical of chronic prostatitis (chronic pelvic pain syndrome). Acute bacterial prostatitis would be febrile and unwell. Source: NICE CKS Prostatitis (UK).
why_wrong: A. Epididymo-orchitis causes acute scrotal pain and swelling. C. Acute bacterial prostatitis causes fever, rigors and a tender prostate over days. D. Benign prostatic enlargement is rare at this age and causes voiding symptoms, not pain on ejaculation. E. A bladder stone causes intermittent pain and haematuria related to movement, not this pattern.
pearl: Chronic prostatitis is a clinical diagnosis based on symptoms of at least three months with negative urine testing.
thinking: Months of pelvic pain and urinary symptoms  ↓  No fever or systemic illness  ↓  Negative urine tests  ↓  Chronic prostatitis
exam_trap: Giving repeated antibiotics for every pelvic pain in a man without evidence of infection.
takeaway: Persistent pelvic pain and urinary symptoms without systemic infection suggest chronic prostatitis.
notes: Source options included testicular torsion and appendicitis; replaced with closer urological distractors. No clinical error. Near live items are female pelvic pain/UTI, not this. Standard teaching, not re-fetched.
sources: NICE CKS Prostatitis (relied on, not re-fetched)

stem:
A 66-year-old woman was started on oral antibiotics by her GP for suspected diverticulitis two days ago. She returns to the emergency department because the pain has spread across the whole lower abdomen. She is febrile, her pulse is 118/min and her blood pressure is low. The abdomen is rigid with guarding.

Which complication should be suspected?

options.A: Diverticulitis that is simply responding slowly to oral treatment
options.B: Faecal loading causing colonic distension and low-grade fever
options.C: A flare of irritable bowel syndrome during the antibiotic course
options.D: Antibiotic-associated colitis as the only explanation for the findings
options.E: Perforated diverticulum with generalised peritonitis and sepsis

correct_answer: E. Perforated diverticulum with generalised peritonitis and sepsis
why_correct: Spreading pain with fever, rigidity, guarding and hypotension in a person with diverticulitis indicates perforation with peritonitis and sepsis. NICE lists abdominal rigidity and guarding as signs of perforation and peritonitis, and altered haemodynamics as signs of sepsis. This needs emergency admission, sepsis management and urgent surgical review. Source: NICE NG147, Diverticular disease, 2019.
why_wrong: A. Slow response would not cause a rigid abdomen with shock, and the picture is of deterioration rather than a sluggish improvement. B. Constipation does not produce guarding, fever of this degree or hypotension. C. IBS does not cause fever, peritonism or haemodynamic instability. D. Antibiotic-associated colitis can cause pain and fever, but rigidity with guarding and shock point to perforation and peritonitis until proven otherwise.
pearl: Rigidity, guarding and shock on a background of diverticulitis mean perforation and sepsis, not a slow treatment response.
thinking: Known or suspected diverticulitis worsening on treatment  ↓  Generalised rigidity, guarding and low blood pressure  ↓  Think perforation with peritonitis and sepsis  ↓  Emergency resuscitation and urgent surgical review
exam_trap: Assuming that a worsening patient on oral antibiotics just needs more time, or attributing fever and pain to constipation or IBS.
takeaway: Diverticulitis with rigidity, guarding and shock is a perforation until proven otherwise.
notes: Vignette rebuilt around failure of outpatient treatment; key and learning point unchanged. NG147 wording checked (abdominal rigidity and guarding = bowel perforation and peritonitis; hypotension/raised heart rate = sepsis). No numbers used.

presentation: Appendicitis not excluded by normal blood tests
stem:
A 24-year-old woman has had 14 hours of abdominal pain that began around her umbilicus and has moved to the right iliac fossa. She has lost her appetite, felt nauseated and has a low-grade fever. Her periods are regular and a pregnancy test is negative. Her white cell count is reported as normal.

Which principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Gynaecological causes are more common in young women, so appendicitis can be set aside
options.B: Appendicitis remains likely, so keep reassessing her despite these normal blood test results
options.C: A normal white cell count excludes appendicitis and she can safely be discharged home
options.D: Appendicitis cannot be considered unless the temperature is clearly above the fever threshold
options.E: Regular bowel habit makes appendicitis very unlikely, so no surgical review is needed

correct_answer: B. Appendicitis remains likely, so keep reassessing her despite these normal blood test results
why_correct: Migratory pain with anorexia, nausea and low-grade fever in the right iliac fossa is classical for appendicitis, and the diagnosis is clinical. The NHS notes there is no test that can always show whether appendicitis is present, so normal blood results do not exclude it and she should be reassessed by the surgical team. Source: NHS, Appendicitis, 2023.
