why_wrong: A. Young women do have gynaecological causes of pelvic pain, but this does not remove appendicitis from the differential when the history is classical. C. No single blood test excludes appendicitis, so a normal white cell count cannot be used to discharge her. D. A high temperature is not required; fever is often absent or mild in early appendicitis. E. Bowel habit is often normal in appendicitis, and surgical review is still needed.
pearl: Appendicitis is a clinical diagnosis, and a normal white cell count or regular bowel habit does not rule it out.
thinking: Migratory right iliac fossa pain with anorexia and nausea  ↓  Classical history for appendicitis  ↓  Normal blood tests do not exclude it  ↓  Keep it on the differential and arrange senior surgical reassessment
exam_trap: Being falsely reassured by a normal white cell count or by the patient being a young woman with possible gynaecological causes.
takeaway: Do not exclude appendicitis on the basis of normal blood tests, sex or bowel habit.
notes: New vignette (migratory pain, normal WCC, negative pregnancy test). The AKT item cited only 'NICE guidance on acute abdominal presentations', so the NHS appendicitis page was used (states no test can always show appendicitis). No NICE appendicitis guideline exists; claim worded as a clinical-diagnosis principle with no numbers. Differs from live BX930/S001 (which ask diagnosis/appendicectomy).

presentation: Visible haematuria in a woman taking aspirin
stem:
A 71-year-old woman notices bright red urine on one occasion and then again two days later. She has no pain, frequency or burning, and she takes low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention after a previous stroke. A urine dipstick shows no nitrites or leucocytes and a urine culture is negative.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Stop the aspirin and repeat the urine test once the bleeding has settled
options.B: Treat as a presumed urinary infection with a short course of antibiotics
options.C: Advise increased fluid intake and review only if the bleeding recurs
options.D: Arrange a routine renal ultrasound scan and review the result in clinic
options.E: Refer urgently on the suspected cancer pathway despite the aspirin use

correct_answer: E. Refer urgently on the suspected cancer pathway despite the aspirin use
why_correct: Unexplained visible haematuria without urinary tract infection in an adult aged 45 or over meets NICE NG12 criteria for a suspected cancer pathway referral for bladder cancer. NG12 makes no exception for people taking antiplatelet treatment, so the bleeding remains unexplained until it has been investigated. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026), recommendation 1.6.4.
why_wrong: A. Aspirin may add to bleeding but is not an acceptable explanation, and stopping a secondary-prevention drug would also delay investigation. B. Dipstick and culture show no infection, so antibiotics are not appropriate. C. Fluids and watchful waiting would delay assessment for bladder or kidney cancer. D. An ultrasound alone does not assess the bladder, and a routine clinic review is too slow for suspected cancer.
pearl: Visible haematuria without infection in an older adult needs a suspected cancer pathway referral, even if the patient takes aspirin.
thinking: Painless visible haematuria, infection excluded  ↓  Older adult, so bladder or renal cancer is the concern  ↓  Antiplatelet drug is not an explanation  ↓  Suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: Attributing the bleeding to aspirin and stopping or waiting instead of investigating.
takeaway: Do not blame antiplatelets or anticoagulants for visible haematuria; investigate for cancer.
notes: New vignette (woman, aspirin) so it differs from live PAQ15108 (63F, no anticoagulant, asks diagnosis), BX525, NEP018, DR014. No day count used for the referral. NG12 1.6.4 verified: age 45+ with unexplained visible haematuria without UTI.

presentation: Shocked patient with acute abdominal pain
stem:
A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden, severe abdominal pain. He is pale and sweaty, his pulse is 128/min and his blood pressure is low. His abdomen is diffusely very tender.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange a CT of the abdomen and review the result the following morning
options.B: Give analgesia and keep him in for review on the morning ward round
options.C: Begin resuscitation and involve the senior surgical team immediately
options.D: Book an urgent outpatient ultrasound scan for later in the week
options.E: Start antibiotics and refer him to the gastroenterology team for review

correct_answer: C. Begin resuscitation and involve the senior surgical team immediately
why_correct: Severe abdominal pain with pallor, tachycardia, hypotension and marked tenderness indicates shock from a possible surgical emergency such as perforation, ischaemia or a ruptured aneurysm. Resuscitation and senior surgical input take priority over establishing the exact diagnosis. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (prompt recognition and escalation of the acutely unwell, hypotensive patient); NHS, Abdominal aortic aneurysm (a ruptured aneurysm needs emergency surgery).
why_wrong: A. Waiting overnight for CT review delays treatment of a shocked, possibly bleeding or perforated patient. B. Analgesia alone and a morning review is unsafe for a haemodynamically unstable patient. D. Outpatient ultrasound has no place in a shocked patient. E. Antibiotics and gastroenterology referral miss the immediate need for resuscitation and a surgical opinion.
pearl: A shocked patient with an acute abdomen needs resuscitation and a senior surgeon first, diagnosis second.
thinking: Acute abdominal pain with shock  ↓  Treat as a surgical emergency  ↓  Resuscitate, call senior surgeon  ↓  Imaging only once safe and not delaying care
exam_trap: Choosing a diagnostic test or ward-round review before stabilising the patient.
takeaway: Resuscitate first and call a senior surgeon when an acute abdomen is accompanied by shock.
notes: New vignette; learning point is the prioritisation (ABCDE and senior surgery), not any specific cause. NICE has no single acute-abdomen guideline, so NHS AAA and NG253 pages were opened; a reviewer may wish to cite a Royal College of Surgeons emergency laparotomy source. Differs from live ACU027 (pulsatile mass AAA) and BX415.

stem:
A 49-year-old woman finds a new lump in her right breast. On examination the overlying skin puckers when she raises her arms above her head, and the lump feels firm and fixed.

What does this finding most strongly suggest?

options.A: A simple fluid-filled cyst, which does not tether the skin at all
options.B: Possible breast cancer tethering the skin, needing urgent assessment
options.C: A fibroadenoma, which is usually smooth and freely mobile
options.D: Benign fibrocystic change, which gives cyclical lumpiness and soreness
options.E: Mastitis from a blocked duct, which is red, warm and tender

correct_answer: B. Possible breast cancer tethering the skin, needing urgent assessment
why_correct: Skin tethering or dimpling over a firm, fixed lump can occur when a tumour involves the tissues beneath the skin and suggests breast cancer. NICE advises a suspected cancer pathway referral for an unexplained breast lump in people aged 30 and over, and to consider it for skin changes that suggest breast cancer. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. A simple cyst is smooth and mobile and does not pull on the skin. C. A fibroadenoma is classically a mobile, smooth lump, not a fixed lump with dimpling. D. Fibrocystic change causes cyclical tenderness and nodularity, not tethering. E. Mastitis causes redness, warmth and tenderness, not a fixed lump with skin puckering.
pearl: Skin dimpling with a firm fixed lump should be treated as breast cancer until assessment proves otherwise.
thinking: New breast lump  ↓  Skin tethering with fixed firm lump  ↓  Think cancer involving deeper structures  ↓  Suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: Choosing a benign cause because the lump is painless or the woman is premenopausal.
takeaway: Skin dimpling over a breast lump suggests malignancy and needs urgent assessment.
notes: Verified NG12 1.4.1/1.4.2 (breast lump aged 30+, skin changes suggesting breast cancer). New vignette (49F, dimpling on arm raising). Distinct from live S047/S009 (irregular lump, referral) because the learning point is the sign.

stem:
A 27-year-old man has had a painless, firm swelling in one testis for a month. Scrotal ultrasound shows a solid mass within the testis and the urology team plan an orchidectomy. Blood is taken beforehand for hCG and LDH and for one further tumour marker that can be raised in non-seminomatous germ cell tumours.

Which further marker is this?

options.A: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
options.B: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)
options.C: Cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9)
options.D: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
options.E: Cancer antigen 125 (CA 125)

correct_answer: D. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
why_correct: Alpha-fetoprotein can be raised in non-seminomatous germ cell tumours but is not raised in pure seminoma. AFP, hCG and LDH are taken before orchidectomy because they support diagnosis, staging and prognosis and are used again in follow-up. Normal markers do not exclude a tumour. Source: Macmillan Cancer Support, Testicular cancer tumour markers (UK), and NHS testicular cancer tests.
why_wrong: A. PSA is a marker for prostate disease and has no role in testicular germ cell tumours. B. CEA is mainly used in colorectal cancer follow-up. C. CA 19-9 is associated with pancreatobiliary cancer. E. CA 125 is used in suspected ovarian cancer.
pearl: AFP, hCG and LDH are the three testicular tumour markers; AFP rises in non-seminoma but not in pure seminoma.
thinking: Solid intratesticular mass in a young man  ↓  Germ cell tumour likely  ↓  Take AFP, hCG and LDH before orchidectomy
exam_trap: Choosing an organ-specific marker for another cancer (PSA, CA 125, CA 19-9) because the name is familiar.
takeaway: For a suspected testicular tumour, send AFP, hCG and LDH before surgery.
notes: Original asked which marker can be raised in some testicular cancers; re-angled to the pre-orchidectomy blood set. Key unchanged and consistent with UK patient-information sources; no movable threshold. NICE NG12 only covers referral, so Macmillan/NHS used for the marker statement. Distractors lengthened so the key is not the longest.

stem:
A 23-year-old man who runs long distances sees red urine after a race. It clears by the next day. He has no urinary symptoms, no recent illness and takes no regular medicines. He asks whether he can simply put it down to the running.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Check urine, blood pressure and kidney function to look for a cause
options.B: Reassure him that exercise is always the explanation and offer no follow-up
options.C: Prescribe empirical antibiotics for a presumed infection without testing urine
options.D: Make a suspected cancer pathway referral automatically at his age
options.E: Advise him to ignore any further episodes unless he develops pain

correct_answer: A. Check urine, blood pressure and kidney function to look for a cause
why_correct: Visible haematuria should not be attributed to exercise until other causes have been looked for, particularly if it persists or recurs. A urine test, blood pressure and renal function check screens for renal and urinary tract causes such as glomerular disease or infection. Exercise-related haematuria is a diagnosis made after other causes are considered. Source: NHS blood in urine guidance and NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: B. Assuming exercise is always the cause risks missing renal or urological disease. C. Antibiotics without a urine test treat a possible infection blindly and do not look for other causes. D. NICE advises a suspected cancer pathway referral for unexplained visible haematuria from the age of 45, not routinely in a young adult. E. Ignoring recurrence delays diagnosis of a treatable cause.
pearl: Never label visible haematuria as exercise-related until other causes have been sought.
thinking: Visible haematuria in a young adult  ↓  Exercise is a diagnosis of exclusion  ↓  Test urine, blood pressure and renal function
exam_trap: Accepting a convenient explanation (running) and stopping the assessment.
takeaway: Visible haematuria always needs a cause looked for, even after exercise.
notes: Original key retained (assess for underlying cause); options reworded and made specific. The age-45 cancer-pathway threshold in NG12 appears only in a distractor explanation, not as the key. CKS haematuria URL returned 404 so NHS and NG12 used.

stem:
A 50-year-old man with gallstone pancreatitis is becoming sicker on the high-dependency unit. Nursing staff notice a bruise-like bluish discolouration of the skin surrounding his navel.

What is this clinical sign called?

options.A: Cullen sign
options.B: Grey Turner sign
options.C: Trousseau sign of malignancy
options.D: Courvoisier sign
options.E: Murphy sign

correct_answer: A. Cullen sign
why_correct: Bluish ecchymosis around the umbilicus is Cullen sign. It is sometimes associated with complicated haemorrhagic pancreatitis, although it is rare, so it should prompt senior review. Source: NICE CKS, Pancreatitis - acute (assessment), 2021.
why_wrong: B. Grey Turner sign is bruising over the flanks. C. Trousseau sign of malignancy is migratory thrombophlebitis, classically with pancreatic cancer. D. Courvoisier sign is a palpable non-tender gallbladder with jaundice. E. Murphy sign is inspiratory arrest on palpation of the right upper quadrant in cholecystitis.
pearl: Cullen is around the umbilicus; Grey Turner is in the flanks.
thinking: Bruising around the umbilicus  ↓  Severe pancreatitis with retroperitoneal bleeding  ↓  Cullen sign
exam_trap: Mixing up Cullen and Grey Turner signs.
takeaway: Periumbilical ecchymosis in pancreatitis is Cullen sign.
notes: New vignette, same fact and key. CKS assessment page confirms both signs and their rarity. Distractor C lengthened so the key is not the longest option.

stem:
A woman admitted with alcohol-related severe pancreatitis is reviewed on the ward round. Her team notes extensive bruise-like discolouration of the skin of both loins.

What is this clinical sign called?

options.A: Grey Turner sign
options.B: Cullen sign
options.C: Trousseau sign of malignancy
options.D: Courvoisier sign
options.E: Chvostek sign

correct_answer: A. Grey Turner sign
why_correct: Ecchymosis of the flanks is Grey Turner sign. It reflects blood tracking in the retroperitoneum and is occasionally seen in severe haemorrhagic pancreatitis. It marks severe disease and calls for senior and critical care input. Source: NICE CKS, Pancreatitis - acute (assessment), 2021.
why_wrong: B. Cullen sign is bruising around the umbilicus. C. Trousseau sign of malignancy is migratory thrombophlebitis. D. Courvoisier sign is a palpable non-tender gallbladder with jaundice. E. Chvostek sign is facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve in hypocalcaemia.
pearl: Grey Turner is in the flanks; Cullen is around the umbilicus.
thinking: Bruising of the loins  ↓  Retroperitoneal haemorrhage in severe pancreatitis  ↓  Grey Turner sign
exam_trap: Confusing the two eponyms for abdominal wall bruising.
takeaway: Flank bruising in severe pancreatitis is Grey Turner sign.
notes: New vignette; key unchanged. Same sources as N3021. Written as a separate fact from N3021 (opposite site).

stem:
A 30-year-old man is hit in the face by a squash ball. The next day he sees double when he looks upwards, and the skin of his cheek and upper lip feels numb. His visual acuity is normal.

What is the most likely injury?

options.A: Orbital floor fracture
options.B: Traumatic optic neuropathy
options.C: Subconjunctival haemorrhage
options.D: Isolated nasal bone fracture
options.E: Retinal detachment

correct_answer: A. Orbital floor fracture
why_correct: A blow-out fracture of the orbital floor can trap or restrict the inferior orbital tissues and muscles, causing diplopia on upward gaze. The infraorbital nerve runs in the floor, so cheek and upper lip numbness can occur. Normal acuity makes optic nerve injury less likely. Source: NHS Scotland Right Decisions, ENT, Dental and Max Fax guidance (2024).
why_wrong: B. Traumatic optic neuropathy reduces vision and does not cause upgaze diplopia. C. A subconjunctival haemorrhage is a red patch and does not explain the double vision. D. An isolated nasal fracture causes nasal deformity and bleeding and does not cause diplopia or cheek numbness. E. Retinal detachment causes flashes and a field defect and does not cause diplopia or numbness.
pearl: Upgaze diplopia plus infraorbital numbness after blunt eye trauma is an orbital floor fracture.
thinking: Blunt eye injury  ↓  Diplopia on upgaze and cheek numbness  ↓  Orbital floor (blow-out) fracture
exam_trap: Assuming a normal visual acuity excludes serious orbital injury.
takeaway: Think blow-out fracture when double vision on looking up follows blunt orbital trauma.
notes: New vignette (squash ball); key unchanged and confirmed by NHS Scotland guidance. Overlap with N3511 is deliberate (that item tests the nerve).

stem:
A 40-year-old woman is punched on the side of the face. Over the next day her cheek looks flatter than the other side, the skin beneath her eye is numb and she can open her mouth only a short way because of pain.

Which injury is most likely?

options.A: Isolated nasal bone fracture
options.B: Mandibular condyle fracture
options.C: Zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture
options.D: Dentoalveolar fracture of the upper incisors
options.E: Isolated orbital roof fracture

correct_answer: C. Zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture
why_correct: A zygomatic complex fracture produces flattening of the cheek, a step at the infraorbital rim and numbness from infraorbital nerve involvement. Mouth opening may be restricted. Source: NHS Scotland Right Decisions, ENT, Dental and Max Fax guidance (2024), and a UK NHS oral and maxillofacial patient leaflet on zygomatic fractures.
why_wrong: A. A nasal fracture causes nasal deformity and epistaxis. B. A condylar fracture causes pre-auricular pain and malocclusion but not cheek flattening or infraorbital numbness. D. A dentoalveolar fracture damages teeth and the alveolar ridge. E. An isolated orbital roof fracture would cause forehead or neurological features, not cheek flattening.
pearl: Flat cheek, infraorbital numbness and restricted mouth opening: think zygomatic fracture.
thinking: Facial blow  ↓  Flat cheek, infraorbital numbness, limited mouth opening  ↓  Zygomatic complex fracture
exam_trap: Picking a mandibular fracture because mouth opening is painful.
takeaway: Cheek flattening with infraorbital numbness points to a zygomatic fracture.
notes: New vignette; key unchanged. Source cited confirms flattening of the zygomatic eminence, infraorbital step and restricted mouth opening. Explanatory statement kept to what the sources state.

stem:
A 19-year-old man is punched on the jaw during a fight. He has pain on chewing and says his teeth no longer meet properly. There is bruising under the tongue and tenderness along the lower jaw.

Which injury should be suspected?

options.A: Orbital floor blow-out fracture
options.B: Isolated nasal bone fracture
options.C: Acute parotitis from a salivary stone
options.D: Fracture of the lower jaw bone
options.E: Dental abscess with facial swelling

correct_answer: D. Fracture of the lower jaw bone
why_correct: Jaw trauma with tenderness along the mandible, an altered bite and sublingual bruising strongly suggests a mandibular fracture. The bite should be checked and the fracture discussed with the oral and maxillofacial surgery team. Fractures through the tooth-bearing area are treated as open. Source: NHS Scotland Right Decisions, ENT, Dental and Max Fax guidance (2024).
why_wrong: A. An orbital floor fracture causes diplopia and cheek numbness. B. A nasal fracture causes nasal swelling and deformity. C. Parotitis causes swelling in front of the ear without a change in the bite after trauma. E. A dental abscess arises from infection and not from a direct blow.
pearl: Altered bite plus sublingual bruising after jaw trauma means mandibular fracture.
thinking: Blow to the jaw  ↓  Altered bite and floor-of-mouth bruising  ↓  Mandibular fracture
exam_trap: Treating a change in bite as a minor dental problem.
takeaway: Ask about the bite after facial trauma; a change suggests a mandibular fracture.
notes: New vignette; key unchanged. Easy retained.

stem:
A cyclist falls onto the handlebars and CT shows a fracture through the floor of the right orbit. He has numbness of the lower eyelid, the side of the nose and the upper lip on that side.

Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?

options.A: Infraorbital nerve
options.B: Supraorbital nerve
options.C: Mental nerve
options.D: Lingual nerve
options.E: Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve

correct_answer: A. Infraorbital nerve
why_correct: The infraorbital nerve, a branch of the maxillary nerve, runs along the floor of the orbit and supplies the lower eyelid, side of the nose, cheek and upper lip. A fracture of the orbital floor can bruise or divide it. Numbness often improves over several months. Source: NHS oral and maxillofacial surgery patient leaflet, Royal United Hospitals Bath, Zygomatic fractures.
why_wrong: B. The supraorbital nerve supplies the forehead and upper eyelid. C. The mental nerve supplies the chin and lower lip. D. The lingual nerve supplies sensation to the front of the tongue. E. The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve is motor to the lower lip and does not cause sensory loss.
pearl: Infraorbital nerve injury gives numbness of the cheek, side of the nose and upper lip after orbital floor fracture.
thinking: Fracture through the orbital floor  ↓  Sensory loss in the infraorbital distribution  ↓  Infraorbital nerve
exam_trap: Choosing a facial nerve because the injury is on the face.
takeaway: Cheek and upper lip numbness after orbital floor fracture is infraorbital nerve injury.
notes: New vignette and options; key unchanged. Difficult kept. Overlap with N3496 is intentional (nerve rather than diagnosis). Anatomy statements are standard; the leaflet source was read via extracted text.

stem:
A 66-year-old man wears a hearing aid in his left ear and has had two weeks of a blocked sensation and muffled hearing on that side. He has no pain or discharge. Otoscopy shows the canal filled with dark material and the eardrum cannot be seen.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Impacted earwax
options.B: Otosclerosis
options.C: Vestibular schwannoma
options.D: Ménière disease
options.E: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss

correct_answer: A. Impacted earwax
why_correct: Wax filling the canal blocks sound conduction, causing muffled hearing and a blocked feeling, and hearing aid use is a common contributor. NICE advises excluding impacted wax and acute infection before audiological assessment of hearing difficulty. Hearing usually improves once the wax is removed. Source: NICE NG98, Hearing loss in adults (2018), and NHS earwax build-up.
why_wrong: B. Otosclerosis causes gradual conductive loss with a normal drum and canal. C. A vestibular schwannoma causes unilateral sensorineural loss and tinnitus with a normal canal. D. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating loss. E. Sudden sensorineural loss has a normal view of the drum.
pearl: Look in the canal first: wax is a common reversible cause of conductive hearing loss.
thinking: Blocked muffled ear  ↓  Canal obstructed by wax  ↓  Impacted earwax
exam_trap: Pursuing audiology or imaging before examining the canal.
takeaway: Check for wax before investigating unilateral hearing loss.
notes: New vignette (hearing aid user); key unchanged. Sources confirm wax exclusion step and symptoms.

stem:
A 34-year-old teacher has a hoarse, croaky voice that began three days after a head cold with a sore throat and cough. She is afebrile, swallowing normally, not drooling and has no noisy breathing or breathlessness.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Acute viral laryngitis
options.B: Acute epiglottitis
options.C: Peritonsillar abscess
options.D: Acute bacterial tracheitis
options.E: Laryngeal carcinoma

correct_answer: A. Acute viral laryngitis
why_correct: Hoarseness after a viral upper respiratory tract infection, with no airway compromise, is typical of acute laryngitis, which usually settles on its own with voice rest and fluids. The absence of stridor, drooling and dysphagia makes epiglottitis and abscess unlikely. Persistent unexplained hoarseness in an older adult would need suspected cancer pathway assessment instead. Source: NHS laryngitis and NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: B. Epiglottitis presents with severe sore throat, drooling and airway distress. C. A peritonsillar abscess causes unilateral throat pain, trismus and a muffled voice. D. Bacterial tracheitis causes high fever, stridor and toxicity. E. Laryngeal carcinoma causes persistent hoarseness, not a short illness after a cold.
pearl: Hoarseness after a cold, with no airway signs, is acute laryngitis; persistent hoarseness needs investigation.
thinking: Hoarse voice after a viral illness  ↓  No stridor or dysphagia  ↓  Acute laryngitis
exam_trap: Over-investigating a short viral hoarseness, or under-investigating a persistent one.
takeaway: Self-limiting hoarseness after a cold is laryngitis; persistent hoarseness is not.
notes: New vignette; key unchanged. CKS laryngitis URL returned 404; NHS page and NG12 used.

stem:
A 4-year-old boy has had a smelly discharge from his right ear for several days. He has no fever and his mother says he often pokes small objects into his ears. Otoscopy shows a small blue plastic bead in the canal.

What is the most likely explanation for the discharge?

options.A: Acute otitis media with spontaneous perforation of the drum
options.B: Chronic suppurative otitis media from a long-standing drum perforation
options.C: Acoustic neuroma with secondary ear infection
options.D: Foreign body retained in the ear canal
options.E: Mastoiditis with a subperiosteal abscess

correct_answer: D. Foreign body retained in the ear canal
why_correct: Unilateral offensive discharge in a young child should raise suspicion of a retained foreign body, and here one is visible. The object irritates and infects the canal skin. Referral for removal, under general anaesthetic if it cannot be removed safely, is usual. Source: NHS Scotland Right Decisions, ENT, Dental and Max Fax guidance (2024), and NHS earache.
why_wrong: A. Acute otitis media with perforation causes fever and preceding earache and the object would not explain it. B. Chronic suppurative otitis media follows long-standing disease, not a visible bead in an otherwise well child. C. Acoustic neuroma is rare in children and does not cause discharge. E. Mastoiditis causes fever, a protruding ear and postauricular swelling.
pearl: Unilateral smelly ear or nose discharge in a young child: look for a foreign body.
thinking: Child with unilateral offensive discharge  ↓  Object seen in canal  ↓  Retained foreign body
exam_trap: Reaching for antibiotics or imaging before removing the object.
takeaway: Think foreign body in a toddler with unilateral offensive discharge.
notes: New vignette; key unchanged. Plan letter D. Live PAQ11193 (pea in ear, management) is a different learning point.

stem:
A 70-year-old man with newly diagnosed prostate cancer and a markedly raised PSA has had persistent, night-time lower back pain for several weeks. His alkaline phosphatase is raised.

Which site of metastasis is most likely to explain the back pain?

options.A: The liver and biliary tree
options.B: The brain and its meninges
options.C: The adrenal glands and kidneys
options.D: The pleura and both lungs
options.E: The spine and pelvic bones

correct_answer: E. The spine and pelvic bones
why_correct: Prostate cancer most commonly spreads to bone, where it causes pain, pathological fractures or spinal cord compression. A raised alkaline phosphatase supports bone involvement. Urgent assessment is needed if features of cord compression appear. Source: NICE CKS, Prostate cancer (background information, complications), and NICE NG131 (2019).
why_wrong: A. Liver metastases are less common and do not explain back pain. B. Brain metastases are uncommon and cause neurological features. C. The adrenal glands are uncommon sites and are usually silent. D. Lung metastases may cause cough or breathlessness rather than back pain.
pearl: Prostate cancer spreads most often to bone, causing pain and risk of cord compression.
thinking: Prostate cancer with night-time back pain  ↓  Raised alkaline phosphatase  ↓  Bone metastases
exam_trap: Choosing a visceral site because the cancer is advanced.
takeaway: Back pain in prostate cancer should be assumed to be bone metastasis until proven otherwise.
notes: Original bare recall; vignette built around bone pain and ALP. Near-live BX1023/PMG071 diagnose a primary from bone pain, not the metastatic site. CKS confirms bone as the commonest site. Key option may be the longest by words: validator decides.

stem:
A 46-year-old man has worked as a shipyard riveter for thirty years and says he struggles to follow a conversation when several people are talking. Both ears are affected, with no pain or discharge. Otoscopy is normal and audiometry shows a bilateral sensorineural loss that is worst at higher frequencies.

What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Otitis media with effusion
options.B: Chronic suppurative otitis media
options.C: Impacted earwax
options.D: Ménière disease with endolymphatic hydrops
options.E: Noise-induced hearing loss

correct_answer: E. Noise-induced hearing loss
why_correct: Long-term occupational noise exposure typically causes bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, with normal otoscopy. Noise exposure is one of the commonest causes of hearing loss, alongside ageing. Prevention through hearing protection and occupational health review is important. Source: NICE CKS, Hearing loss in adults (causes), 2024, and NHS hearing loss.
why_wrong: A. Effusion causes a conductive loss with an abnormal drum. B. Chronic suppurative otitis media has discharge and a perforation. C. Wax would be visible and cause a conductive loss. D. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating, usually unilateral, loss.
pearl: Bilateral high-frequency sensorineural loss in a noisy occupation is noise-induced.
thinking: Years of loud work  ↓  Bilateral high-frequency sensorineural loss  ↓  Noise-induced hearing loss
exam_trap: Missing the occupational history.
takeaway: Take an occupational noise history in anyone with bilateral high-frequency hearing loss.
notes: Age lowered to 46 and audiometry added to separate from age-related loss. Key unchanged. CKS causes page confirms noise as a leading cause.

presentation: Sudden hearing loss with facial droop
stem:
A 61-year-old man woke this morning with muffled hearing in his right ear and has noticed that the right corner of his mouth droops when he smiles. He has no ear pain or discharge.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Immediate ENT assessment, or the stroke pathway if a stroke is suspected
options.B: Book a routine audiology appointment and arrange review in primary care next month
options.C: Prescribe oral antibiotics and arrange a review in a week if no better
options.D: Offer ear syringing at the practice nurse clinic and reassure him
options.E: Start an antihistamine and nasal steroid spray for presumed Eustachian tube dysfunction

correct_answer: A. Immediate ENT assessment, or the stroke pathway if a stroke is suspected
why_correct: Sudden unilateral hearing loss with a same-sided facial droop is a red-flag combination that needs immediate assessment. NICE advises immediate referral to an ear, nose and throat service, or to the local stroke pathway if a stroke is suspected. Treating it as a minor ear problem risks missing a stroke or other serious cause. Source: NICE NG98, Hearing loss in adults (2018), recommendation 1.1.3.
why_wrong: B. Routine audiology is far too slow for sudden loss with a neurological sign. C. Antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of infection. D. Syringing does not explain the facial droop and delays assessment. E. Eustachian tube dysfunction does not cause facial weakness.
pearl: Sudden hearing loss with facial droop needs same-day specialist or stroke assessment.
thinking: Sudden unilateral hearing loss  ↓  Same-sided facial droop  ↓  Immediate ENT or stroke pathway
exam_trap: Treating the ear symptom alone as minor.
takeaway: Never manage sudden hearing loss with neurological signs as routine.
notes: Vignette rewritten. NG98 recommendation is cited directly; wording avoids a time window. Near-live BX319 (sudden loss only) differs by the facial droop.

stem:
A 65-year-old man who feels completely well receives an NHS letter inviting him for a one-off, painless ultrasound scan of his abdomen. He asks his GP what the scan is looking for.

Which condition is the screening test designed to detect?

options.A: Peripheral arterial disease of the legs
options.B: Asymptomatic gallstones in the gallbladder
options.C: Early-stage renal cell carcinoma
options.D: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
options.E: Pancreatic head carcinoma

correct_answer: D. Abdominal aortic aneurysm
why_correct: The NHS abdominal aortic aneurysm screening programme offers a single ultrasound to men in the year they turn 65. Finding an aneurysm early allows monitoring and planned repair, and reduces the risk of rupture. Source: NHS abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) screening, NHS England.
why_wrong: A. Peripheral arterial disease is not screened for by abdominal ultrasound. B. Gallstones are not screened for in well people. C. There is no national renal cancer screening programme. E. There is no national screening programme for pancreatic cancer.
pearl: AAA screening is a one-off abdominal ultrasound offered to men in the year they turn 65.
thinking: Well man invited for abdominal scan  ↓  National screening programme  ↓  AAA screening
exam_trap: Confusing screening with a diagnostic test for symptoms.
takeaway: AAA screening targets men in the year they turn 65 with one ultrasound.
notes: Re-angled from a bare recall. The age of invitation is in the stem but is not the key. Near-live CARD025/S048 test management after a screen result, not the purpose. Source is NHS England patient information.

stem:
A 79-year-old woman is on day 6 after a knee revision operation and is on regular opioids. Two days ago a CT scan showed a grossly dilated caecum and colon with no mechanical blockage, and she was being managed conservatively. This afternoon her pain suddenly worsens, she has a temperature, a fast pulse and a board-like abdomen with rebound tenderness.

Which complication has most likely developed?

options.A: Spontaneous resolution of the colonic dilatation
options.B: Worsening opioid-induced constipation
options.C: Perforation of the grossly distended caecum
options.D: Sigmoid volvulus with a closed loop
options.E: Acute pancreatitis caused by opioid analgesia

correct_answer: C. Perforation of the grossly distended caecum
why_correct: A massively dilated colon, as in acute colonic pseudo-obstruction, has a stretched and poorly perfused wall that can become ischaemic and perforate. Sudden worsening pain with fever, tachycardia and generalised peritonism in this setting signals perforation with peritonitis, which needs urgent senior surgical review and resuscitation. Source: UK tertiary-centre cohort of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ann Med Surg 2026); NHS peritonitis guidance.
why_wrong: A. Resolution would bring less pain and a softer abdomen, not peritonism and sepsis. B. Constipation does not cause rebound tenderness, rigidity or fever. D. Volvulus would be a mechanical obstruction, which the earlier CT excluded, and does not explain the new peritonitis in this context. E. Pancreatitis causes upper abdominal pain radiating to the back and would not follow this course.
pearl: In colonic pseudo-obstruction, new peritonism or fever means perforation or ischaemia until proven otherwise.
thinking: Known grossly dilated colon without obstruction  ↓  New fever, tachycardia, rigidity and rebound  ↓  Wall ischaemia and perforation with peritonitis  ↓  Resuscitate and call the surgical team urgently
exam_trap: Assuming that a previously benign, conservatively managed distension will keep behaving benignly.
takeaway: Pseudo-obstruction with sudden peritonism means perforation, an emergency.
notes: Source key (A) is sound; no figures used (the caecal-diameter threshold in the literature was deliberately left out as a movable number). Angle changed from a bare recall to a deterioration vignette. Near-live S056/PAQ15401/PAQ281 test the diagnosis/management of pseudo-obstruction, not the perforation complication. Sources are a recent UK cohort plus an NHS page (no NICE guideline exists).

stem:
A 44-year-old man is assessed in the emergency department with eight hours of severe central abdominal pain that has become constant and generalised. He lies motionless and is breathing shallowly. The examiner wants to decide whether he has peritonitis.

Which examination finding best supports peritoneal inflammation?

options.A: Loud, frequent bowel sounds with colicky pain
options.B: Tightening of the abdomen only when he is anxious
options.C: Restless writhing that eases on changing position
options.D: Reflex rigidity that persists despite distraction
options.E: Generalised bloating with no tenderness on palpation

correct_answer: D. Reflex rigidity that persists despite distraction
why_correct: Peritoneal inflammation causes a reflex, involuntary contraction of the abdominal wall muscles that cannot be relaxed and persists when the patient is distracted. Together with rebound tenderness and a patient lying still, it points to peritonitis and a surgical emergency. Source: standard UK surgical clinical examination teaching (no NICE guideline covers this sign); NHS peritonitis guidance for the clinical context.
why_wrong: A. Hyperactive bowel sounds with colicky pain suggest mechanical obstruction or gastroenteritis, not peritoneal irritation. B. Voluntary guarding from anxiety relaxes when the patient is distracted or reassured. C. Restless writhing is typical of colic from a hollow viscus, whereas peritonitis makes patients lie still. E. Bloating without tenderness does not indicate peritoneal inflammation.
pearl: A rigid abdomen that stays rigid on distraction, with a patient lying still, indicates peritonitis; colic makes patients move.
thinking: Is the muscle tension voluntary or reflex  ↓  Does it persist with distraction and gentle palpation  ↓  Reflex rigidity means peritoneal irritation  ↓  Urgent senior surgical assessment
exam_trap: Mistaking anxious, voluntary guarding or colicky writhing for peritonism.
takeaway: Involuntary, persistent guarding is the hallmark of peritoneal inflammation.
notes: Clinical-sign question; AKT key sound. New vignette, options reworded. Near-live BX415/S044 present a rigid abdomen with shock or free air, a different learning point (diagnosis/management, not discriminating involuntary from voluntary guarding). Only the NHS peritonitis page was opened; it lists peritonitis symptoms but does not describe guarding, so the sign itself rests on standard examination teaching: reviewer please confirm.
sources: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC12658405/fullTextXML (narrative review of surgical decision-making in acute abdomen)

stem:
A 73-year-old woman has a new end colostomy after emergency bowel surgery two days ago. This morning the nurse notes that the stoma, which was moist and bright red yesterday, is now dusky and almost black. It feels cool, there is no bleeding when touched, and she reports growing pain around it.

What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Compromised blood supply to the stoma
options.B: Expected mucosal change as the stoma settles
options.C: Faecal impaction within the stoma
options.D: Peristomal skin infection from the appliance
options.E: Early parastomal hernia formation

correct_answer: A. Compromised blood supply to the stoma
why_correct: A healthy stoma is moist and pink to red because its blood supply is intact. A dusky, dark or black stoma that is cool and does not bleed suggests the blood supply is compromised, and the surgical team must assess it urgently because the bowel may be necrotic. Source: UK NHS hospital trust stoma-care guidance (a stoma should be pink and warm; purple or black needs urgent medical advice).
why_wrong: B. A normal stoma stays pink to red, so dark discolouration is not a normal settling change. C. Impaction causes reduced output and cramps, not a black, cold stoma. D. Skin infection produces redness and discharge on the surrounding skin, not discolouration of the stoma itself. E. A hernia appears as a bulge beside the stoma, not a change in its colour.
pearl: A pale, dusky or black stoma means poor perfusion and needs urgent surgical review, not routine stoma-nurse advice.
thinking: Healthy stoma is pink or red and moist  ↓  Dark, cool, non-bleeding stoma  ↓  Ischaemia of the stoma  ↓  Urgent surgical assessment
exam_trap: Reassuring the patient that stoma colour changes are normal in the first days.
takeaway: A dark purple or black stoma means ischaemia and is urgent.
notes: AKT key sound. New vignette with timing, temperature and bleeding clues. Near-live BX201 (stoma prolapse) and BX212 (parastomal hernia) are different diagnoses. The NHS ileostomy complications page was opened but does not discuss stoma colour or ischaemia, and the colostomy NHS pages could not be loaded, so the key rests on standard stoma-care teaching: reviewer please confirm.

stem:
A 58-year-old man had an ileostomy formed nine days ago and went home yesterday. He returns feeling light-headed on standing, with a dry mouth and passing very little urine. His stoma bag fills repeatedly with large volumes of watery fluid. Blood pressure falls when he stands.

Which complication is most likely?

options.A: Stoma retraction beneath the skin
options.B: Parastomal hernia formation
options.C: Adhesional small bowel obstruction
options.D: Vasovagal episode when emptying the bag
options.E: Fluid and electrolyte depletion

correct_answer: E. Fluid and electrolyte depletion
why_correct: A new ileostomy can produce large volumes of watery output because the colon is no longer absorbing water and electrolytes. Postural dizziness, a dry mouth and low urine output show volume depletion, which may progress to acute kidney injury and needs fluid replacement and review. Source: NHS ileostomy complications guidance (dehydration).
why_wrong: A. Retraction affects appliance fit and leakage, not volume status. B. A hernia causes a bulge beside the stoma, not large volume loss. C. Obstruction would reduce output and cause vomiting and cramps. D. A vasovagal episode would be brief and would not explain high output or reduced urine production.
pearl: High ileostomy output with postural symptoms is dehydration until proven otherwise; check urea, creatinine and electrolytes.
thinking: Large watery stoma output after recent ileostomy  ↓  Postural drop and low urine volume  ↓  Fluid and electrolyte depletion  ↓  Rehydrate and check renal function
exam_trap: Treating dizziness as a vasovagal or medication problem and missing dehydration and kidney injury.
takeaway: High-output ileostomy risks dehydration and electrolyte loss.
notes: AKT key sound. New vignette (timing after discharge, postural signs); no figures. Near-live BX212 is a parastomal hernia item. Separate item UN6464 asks WHY ileostomy patients need fluid (mechanism); this one asks the complication.

stem:
A 50-year-old woman has just gone home after an operation that left her with an ileostomy. At her stoma nurse review she says she never feels thirsty and asks why she has been told to drink more than before.

Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Her kidneys now excrete more urine since the operation
options.B: The colon, which reabsorbs stool water, is bypassed
options.C: The stoma bag draws fluid out of the bowel by suction
options.D: Fluids are needed to keep the stoma from shrinking back
options.E: Her stomach now makes much more fluid than before

correct_answer: B. The colon, which reabsorbs stool water, is bypassed
why_correct: The large bowel normally absorbs most of the water and electrolytes from the stool. With an ileostomy that absorptive segment is bypassed, so fluid and salt losses in the output are larger and dehydration is more likely, even without thirst. Source: NHS ileostomy guidance (dehydration complication; colon bypassed).
why_wrong: A. The kidneys are not directly affected; the extra fluid loss is through the stoma. C. A bag collects output passively and does not suck fluid from the bowel. D. Stoma retraction is not prevented by drinking. E. The stomach does not increase fluid secretion because of an ileostomy.
pearl: No colon means no water reclamation, so ileostomy patients need reliable fluid intake and electrolyte-containing drinks if output is high.
thinking: Which organ reabsorbs stool water  ↓  It is bypassed by an ileostomy  ↓  Output carries more fluid and salt  ↓  Hence advice to keep drinking
exam_trap: Choosing a renal or gastric explanation because fluid and kidneys feel familiar.
takeaway: With an ileostomy the colon no longer reclaims water, so dehydration is the risk.
notes: AKT key sound; new patient-education scenario, options reordered and reworded. No near-live item tests this mechanism.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman has a descending colostomy formed for rectal cancer several months ago. For more than a day nothing has passed into her bag. She now has colicky abdominal pain, a swollen tummy and repeated vomiting. The stoma itself looks pink and healthy.

What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Mechanical bowel obstruction
options.B: Peristomal skin candidiasis spreading under the bag
options.C: Normal pause in function that needs no action
options.D: Gastro-oesophageal reflux causing the vomiting
options.E: Stoma prolapse that needs a larger appliance

correct_answer: A. Mechanical bowel obstruction
why_correct: Absent stoma output with colicky pain, distension and vomiting is the classic picture of bowel obstruction, which may be adhesional or due to recurrent disease. NHS advice says a stoma that is not active with severe cramps, nausea and vomiting needs urgent medical assessment, and surgical review with imaging is needed. Source: NHS ileostomy complications guidance (bowel blockage; urgent advice), which applies equally to a colostomy.
why_wrong: B. Skin candidiasis causes an itchy rash, not absent output and vomiting. C. A pause with pain, distension and vomiting is not normal and must not be dismissed. D. Reflux does not explain absent output and colicky pain. E. Prolapse is a visible protrusion and does not cause this picture.
pearl: No output plus colic, distension and vomiting through a stoma means obstruction until proven otherwise.
thinking: Stoma silent for more than a day  ↓  Colic, distension, vomiting  ↓  Mechanical bowel obstruction  ↓  Urgent surgical review and imaging
exam_trap: Treating it as a skin or appliance problem because the stoma looks healthy.
takeaway: A healthy-looking stoma with no output and obstructive symptoms is a bowel obstruction.
notes: AKT key sound. The NHS page is the ileostomy one; the principle applies equally to colostomy. Near-live BX201 (prolapse) and generic obstruction items test different scenarios (no stoma). The 36 hours is vignette colour, not the key.

stem:
A 55-year-old man is five days after an emergency operation that left him with a colostomy. He avoids looking at the bag, will not let his wife see it, and is tearful, saying he feels disfigured. He is otherwise recovering well.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Explore his concerns and offer stoma nurse and counselling support
options.B: Advise that such feelings settle by themselves and avoid raising them again
options.C: Start an antidepressant today and postpone all stoma teaching until his mood lifts
options.D: Postpone any discussion of how he feels until the stoma has been reversed
options.E: Advise him to concentrate on bag care and leave emotional issues to his family

correct_answer: A. Explore his concerns and offer stoma nurse and counselling support
why_correct: A stoma can affect body image, intimacy and emotional wellbeing as well as everyday practical care. Distress should be explored openly, with specialist stoma nurse input to build practical confidence and access to psychological support when needed, rather than ignored or medicated by default. Source: NHS ileostomy recovery guidance (adjusting; stoma nurse); 2026 open-access review of stoma psychosocial adjustment.
why_wrong: B. Ignoring distress in the hope it settles leaves a treatable problem unaddressed. C. Medication without assessment is premature and delaying stoma teaching hinders independence. D. Many colostomies are permanent, and waiting for reversal leaves him unsupported. E. Delegating to family does not provide professional support and may isolate him.
pearl: Stoma-related distress is common; explore it, involve the stoma nurse and offer psychological support early.
thinking: New stoma with distress about body image  ↓  Normal adjustment or depression needing assessment  ↓  Explore concerns and support practically and emotionally  ↓  Stoma nurse plus psychological support
exam_trap: Choosing medication or avoidance instead of an open conversation with specialist support.
takeaway: Support after stoma formation must address both practical care and emotional wellbeing.
notes: AKT key sound. Source pages cover stoma support only generally: the NHS recovery page and a 2026 open-access review on psychosocial adjustment (body image, anxiety, withdrawal). The key is the longest-looking option category-wise but is not the longest by characters (validator checked).

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has had a red, scaly, crusted rash on her right nipple spreading onto the areola for three months. It has not responded to emollients or a short course of topical steroid. Her left breast and nipple are normal and no lump can be felt.

Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.A: Eczema of the nipple and areola
options.B: Candidal infection of the nipple
options.C: Mondor disease of the breast
options.D: Paget disease of the breast
options.E: Periductal mastitis

correct_answer: D. Paget disease of the breast
why_correct: A persistent eczema-like change affecting one nipple and areola, especially if unresponsive to treatment, suggests Paget disease of the breast, which is associated with an underlying breast cancer. She needs referral to a breast service through the suspected cancer pathway for assessment and biopsy. Source: NHS Paget's disease of the nipple; NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Eczema is usually bilateral, tends to start on the areola rather than the nipple, and responds to emollients and topical steroids. B. Candidal infection is typically bilateral or associated with breastfeeding and responds to antifungals. C. Mondor disease is a tender cord of superficial vein thrombosis on the breast wall, not a nipple rash. E. Periductal mastitis presents with pain, nipple inversion or discharge rather than a scaly rash.
pearl: Unilateral nipple eczema that does not clear with treatment is Paget disease until a breast specialist proves otherwise.
thinking: Scaly rash on one nipple spreading to areola  ↓  No response to emollient and steroid  ↓  Paget disease with possible underlying cancer  ↓  Refer via the suspected cancer pathway
exam_trap: Treating nipple eczema repeatedly with steroids rather than referring when it is unilateral or persistent.
takeaway: Persistent unilateral nipple eczema suggests Paget disease of the breast.
notes: AKT key sound. Patient aged 58 to fit NG12's one-nipple criterion. Near-live PAQ937 is nipple retraction; BX306/BX1031 are unrelated. Option wording changed.

stem:
A 63-year-old man who stopped smoking recently notices a painless lump on the right side of his neck that has slowly enlarged over two months. He has no sore throat or fever. His GP examines it to judge how worrying it is.

Which examination finding would most increase concern about malignancy?

options.A: A soft, fluctuant lump that moves freely
options.B: A hard lump that is fixed to deeper tissues
options.C: A tender swelling that began with a sore throat
options.D: Small mobile nodes on both sides after a cold
options.E: A lump that has been shrinking over several days

correct_answer: B. A hard lump that is fixed to deeper tissues
why_correct: A hard, irregular lymph node or mass that is fixed to deeper tissues, and that persists or enlarges without infection, is concerning for malignancy such as metastatic disease or lymphoma. Adults aged 45 and over with an unexplained neck lump should be considered for suspected cancer pathway referral. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026); hard, fixed nodes as a feature of malignancy is standard examination teaching.
why_wrong: A. Soft, fluctuant, freely mobile lumps are usually cysts or benign swellings. C. Tenderness with a recent infection suggests reactive lymphadenitis. D. Small mobile bilateral nodes during a cold are reactive. E. A lump that is shrinking suggests a reactive or inflammatory cause.
pearl: Hard, fixed, painless and persistent or enlarging neck lumps in older adults need suspected cancer pathway assessment.
thinking: Neck lump in an older ex-smoker  ↓  Which features distinguish reactive from malignant  ↓  Hard and fixed means malignant concern  ↓  Suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: Choosing tenderness as the alarm feature when infective nodes are typically tender.
takeaway: Hardness and fixity, not tenderness, signal malignancy in a neck lump.
notes: AKT key sound. Angle is the examination features, whereas live BX540/BX436 ask next step in a persistent lump with unspecified features; PAQ852 is lymphoma with B symptoms. Only figure is age 45 in the NG12 explanation. The hard/fixed feature itself is not stated in the NG12 page; it rests on standard teaching.

stem:
A 63-year-old man has had looser, more frequent stools for eight weeks. He has no rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss and no previous bowel problems. Abdominal and rectal examination are normal. His GP is tempted to label this irritable bowel syndrome.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange a quantitative faecal immunochemical test in primary care
options.B: Start loperamide for presumed functional diarrhoea and review in several months
options.C: Advise a trial of extra dietary fibre and review in a year
options.D: Prescribe prednisolone for presumed inflammatory colitis
options.E: Send stool culture only and investigate further if bleeding appears

correct_answer: A. Arrange a quantitative faecal immunochemical test in primary care
why_correct: A new persistent change in bowel habit in an adult should not be assumed to be irritable bowel syndrome. NICE recommends offering a quantitative faecal immunochemical test (FIT) in adults with a change in bowel habit to guide referral for suspected colorectal cancer, with a suspected cancer pathway referral if the result is positive. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: B. Empirical loperamide with delayed review risks missing colorectal cancer. C. Fibre advice with review in a year is an unacceptable delay. D. Steroids for presumed colitis are not appropriate without evidence of inflammatory bowel disease. E. Waiting for bleeding before investigating delays diagnosis.
pearl: A persistent new change in bowel habit is a colorectal cancer symptom: test with FIT, not reassure or treat empirically.
thinking: Persistent new bowel habit change in an adult  ↓  Do not label IBS without excluding cancer  ↓  Offer FIT to guide referral  ↓  Positive FIT leads to suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: Diagnosing IBS in a new-onset change in bowel habit in an older adult.
takeaway: Persistent change in bowel habit warrants FIT-guided assessment, not an IBS label.
notes: AKT key sound but vague (no test named). Angled to NG12 1.3.1: FIT for any adult with a change in bowel habit, no cut-off numbers. Near-live GAS066/S049 have rectal bleeding, weight loss and anaemia; PAQ15871 iron-deficiency without bowel symptoms. Reviewer: S049 also mentions a quantitative test; check overlap.

stem:
A 38-year-old man has had two episodes of right upper abdominal pain over three months, each followed by dark urine and yellow eyes. He is afebrile. Liver tests show a cholestatic pattern, and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP, a scan of the bile ducts) shows several stones lying within the common bile duct.

Which term best describes this finding?

options.A: Choledocholithiasis
options.B: Cholelithiasis
options.C: Acute cholecystitis
options.D: Ascending cholangitis
options.E: Nephrolithiasis

correct_answer: A. Choledocholithiasis
why_correct: Stones within the common bile duct are called choledocholithiasis and can cause obstructive jaundice and biliary-type pain. Cholelithiasis refers to stones in the gallbladder. NICE suggests considering MRCP when ultrasound has not detected bile duct stones but the duct is dilated or liver tests are abnormal. Source: NICE CG188, Gallstone disease.
why_wrong: B. Cholelithiasis means gallbladder stones, not stones in the bile duct. C. Acute cholecystitis is gallbladder inflammation with fever and a positive Murphy sign. D. Ascending cholangitis is bile duct infection with fever and rigors, which are absent here. E. Nephrolithiasis means kidney stones.
pearl: Choledocholithiasis means stones in the common bile duct, whereas cholelithiasis means gallbladder stones.
thinking: Locate the stones on imaging  ↓  Common bile duct rather than gallbladder or kidney  ↓  Name the condition: choledocholithiasis  ↓  Recall that afebrile obstruction is not cholangitis
exam_trap: Confusing choledocholithiasis with cholelithiasis because the words look alike.
takeaway: Bile duct stones are choledocholithiasis; gallbladder stones are cholelithiasis.
notes: Terminology item rebuilt with an obstructive-jaundice vignette; live S024 and DT117 test imaging and management. Source key unchanged.

stem:
A 19-year-old man describes vague, poorly localised pain around his umbilicus that began yesterday. About 12 hours later the pain has become sharp and constant in the right iliac fossa and is worse on coughing. A student asks why the site of the pain has changed.

Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Referral of pain along the right phrenic nerve to the groin
options.B: Visceral pain followed by parietal peritoneal irritation
options.C: Movement of a faecolith along the large bowel wall
options.D: Spasm of the small bowel mesentery after vomiting
options.E: Compression of the common bile duct by inflammation

correct_answer: B. Visceral pain followed by parietal peritoneal irritation
why_correct: Early appendiceal inflammation stimulates visceral afferents, giving dull central pain. As inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, somatic nerves localise the pain to the right iliac fossa and movement makes it worse. Source: NHS, Appendicitis (pain starts around the belly button, moves to the lower right and is worse on moving or coughing); the visceral-to-parietal mechanism is standard surgical physiology.
why_wrong: A. Phrenic nerve referral gives shoulder-tip pain, not right iliac fossa pain. C. Faecoliths lodge in the appendix lumen and do not travel along the colon. D. Mesenteric spasm does not explain the localising, movement-related pain. E. Bile duct compression causes jaundice and upper abdominal pain.
pearl: Appendiceal pain starts as central visceral pain and localises to the right iliac fossa once the parietal peritoneum is inflamed.
thinking: Vague central pain first  ↓  Later sharp localised right iliac fossa pain  ↓  Visceral afferents then somatic parietal peritoneal nerves  ↓  Recognise the migration as appendicitis
exam_trap: Choosing referred pain explanations that sound neuroanatomical but do not fit.
takeaway: Migrating pain reflects the shift from visceral to parietal peritoneal involvement.
notes: Live PLAB 1 appendicitis items (S001, BX243, PAQ934) test diagnosis; this tests the mechanism of pain migration. Key unchanged.
